Topic Statement
Disentangling Scale from Targeted Pretraining Depth: Testing the Less-Is-More Hypothesis for Bengali Mathematical Reasoning
Problem Statement
LIMO and s1 demonstrated that a few hundred to a thousand carefully curated examples can elicit strong step-by-step mathematical reasoning in English LLMs — but only under a specific precondition: the base model must already hold dense, relevant knowledge from pretraining. Separately, CaTS showed that a model's own confidence can govern test-time compute allocation more efficiently than fixed sampling, though only via an expensive dedicated calibration-training pipeline. Both paradigms remain untested in genuinely low-resource languages.
The one existing effort at Bengali mathematical reasoning, GanitLLM, bypassed the minimal-data route entirely, using an expensive curriculum-based reinforcement learning pipeline instead. Separately, recent cross-lingual test-time scaling studies present conflicting evidence: MCLM found budget forcing yields only marginal average gains outside English, while a follow-up study found larger models within the same generic multilingual model family do benefit substantially from cross-lingual budget forcing — attributing this to parameter scale. However, because that study only varied model size within one generically multilingual family, scale and targeted low-resource-language pretraining depth were never disentangled; a smaller model with deep, targeted Bengali pretraining was never compared against a larger model with only incidental Bengali exposure.
It remains unknown whether minimal-data reasoning elicitation and cross-lingual test-time scaling depend on raw model scale or on targeted pretraining depth in the specific low-resource language; whether English-derived data-selection criteria identify valuable Bengali training examples; whether elicited reasoning generalizes beyond mathematics in Bengali; and whether a cheap, untrained confidence signal can support test-time compute allocation in Bengali without CaTS's costly calibration pipeline. Without this evidence, Bengali NLP researchers have no basis for choosing minimal, low-cost post-training over expensive reinforcement learning, and no clear understanding of what actually determines whether cheap methods succeed or fail in low-resource settings.
Gap Synthesis Paragraph
Across the whole matrix, two separate research threads exist side by side but have never actually been connected. One thread is about test-time scaling and confidence — CaTS, Thought Calibration, MetaFaith, and the "Revisiting Test-Time Scaling of o1-like Models" paper — and it shows that even in English, these tricks are shakier than people assume: self-revision only fixes a wrong answer less than 10% of the time, correct answers tend to be shorter than incorrect ones, and Snell et al. found that more test-time compute mostly helps on easy questions, not hard ones. So "think longer" isn't a guaranteed win even in the best-case language. The other thread is about Bengali reasoning specifically — GanitLLM, TigerLLM, TituLLM, Qi et al., Yong et al. — and here the papers actually disagree with each other in a way nobody's resolved: TigerLLM found that a small model with a good, targeted Bengali corpus beat a much bigger general multilingual model, suggesting quality of targeted pretraining matters most. Yong et al. found that bigger models handled Bengali better under budget forcing, suggesting scale matters most. And TituLLM's own results split the difference in an odd way — its Bengali-focused pretraining helped a lot on commonsense-style tasks but did nothing for broad knowledge tasks like Bangla MMLU, meaning pretraining depth might help some capabilities and not others, not just "more depth = more of everything." Nobody has tried to reconcile these by directly comparing backbones that differ in how targeted their Bengali pretraining is, at similar sizes, on the same reasoning task. On top of that, the data-selection side of this (LESS) has never been tested against LIMO's simpler keyword-based curation in Bengali at all, and the confidence side (CaTS, MetaFaith, Kadavath) has never been tested outside English either. So the actual gap isn't just "nobody's tested LIMO in Bengali" — it's that the field has three separate, half-conflicting explanations (scale, quality, capability-specific pretraining) for what makes low-resource reasoning elicitation work, and nobody has run the one experiment that would tell them apart.



P3 Draft Research Questions

* RQ1 (The Brain vs. Vocabulary Test): Does an AI’s ability to "reason" in Bengali depend more on its raw size (Scale) or on how deeply it was taught Bengali during its initial training (Targeted Depth)? We will test this by giving a large-but-shallow model (TigerLLM-9B) and a small-but-deep model (TituLLM-3B) the exact same reasoning lessons.
* RQ2 (The Logic Transfer Test): If we teach a model to be better at Bengali math, does that logic carry over to other non-math tasks? We will evaluate the models on real-world, high-stakes Bengali exam questions (B-REASO) to see if they’ve learned to "think" or just "calculate."
* RQ3 (The "Gut Feeling" Test): Can a model accurately judge its own confidence in Bengali to save time? We will test if a simple Bengali prompt (e.g., "How sure are you?") can tell the model when to stop thinking, or if Bengali models require expensive, specialized training to be truly "self-aware" of their mistakes.



P3 Hypotheses or Research Propositions

* H1 (Relates to RQ1): We propose that Targeted Depth is more important than Scale. Even though TituLLM-3B is smaller, its massive Bengali pretraining will provide the "linguistic connective tissue" needed to express complex thoughts, allowing it to outperform the larger TigerLLM-9B after fine-tuning.
* H2 (Relates to RQ2): We expect Partial Transfer. The models will likely show some improvement on general Bengali exams, but the gains won't be as big as they are in math, because "math-logic" only partially overlaps with "exam-logic."
* H3 (Relates to RQ3): We propose that Untrained Confidence is Imperfect. The models will be able to save some "thinking time" by judging their own work, but they won't be as efficient as models that have been specifically trained to calibrate their confidence.



P3 Variables, Constructs, or Key Concepts

* Independent Variables (What we change): The specific AI backbone (TigerLLM-9B vs. TituLLM-3B); the amount of targeted Bengali pretraining; and the "thinking budget" (fixed time vs. stopping when confident).
* Dependent Variables (What we measure): Accuracy on Bengali math benchmarks (Bn-MGSM, Bn-MSVAMP, etc.); accuracy on high-stakes Bengali exams (B-REASO); and Bengali Language Adherence (does the AI stay in Bengali while thinking?).
* Core Concepts: Reasoning Elicitation (waking up the logic already inside a model); Test-Time Compute (giving the AI extra seconds to "think" before answering); and Calibration (how well the AI’s confidence matches its actual accuracy).



P3 Planned Study or Evaluation Design

* Controlled experiment: (We are holding the training data and method fixed while varying the model backbone to isolate the effect of scale vs. depth).
* Model design and evaluation: (We are building a custom "budget-forcing" loop to control how long the models think).
* NLP experiment: (We are testing linguistic behaviors like language switching and reasoning traces).
* Benchmarking or performance evaluation: (We are testing against established and natively-authored Bengali datasets).



P3 RQ to Method Alignment

* RQ1 Alignment: We will fine-tune both models on an identical, tiny "cheat sheet" (LIMO-style) of 1,000 high-quality Bengali problems. By comparing their scores, we can see if the "Big" model or the "Deeply Taught" model benefits more from the training.
* RQ2 Alignment: We will take the models trained in RQ1 and, without any further training, test them on the B-REASO benchmark. By comparing the "math gain" to the "exam gain," we can measure how well the logic transfers.
* RQ3 Alignment: We will run two versions of the models: one that thinks for a fixed number of steps, and one that stops if it "feels" confident. We will compare their accuracy and the number of "thinking tokens" used to see which is more efficient.



P3 Validity Threats and Mitigation Plan

* Confounding Differences (Model Engines): The two models use different "engines" (Gemma-2 vs. Llama-3.2). Mitigation: We will clearly document these architectural differences and frame our findings as a "directional comparison" rather than a perfect causal law.
* Construct Validity (Measuring "Depth"): Using "token count" to measure pretraining depth is an estimate. Mitigation: We will report the "Bengali Density" (tokens per parameter) to give a more accurate picture of how "saturated" each model is in the language.
* Dataset/Translation Bias: Translated math problems might favor models that were trained more on English. Mitigation: We will report results for translated benchmarks and natively-authored benchmarks separately to see if there is a "translation advantage."
* Implementation Bugs: Custom "thinking loops" are prone to errors. Mitigation: We will manually spot-check the AI's "inner monologue" (reasoning traces) to ensure the logic isn't just looping or repeating nonsense.

These differ not only in scale but also in base architecture (Gemma-2 vs Llama-3.2) and the depth of Bengali pretraining simultaneously. Based on the search results, here's what I found about GanitLLM and Bengali mathematical reasoning:

## GanitLLM Overview

GanitLLM is a Bengali mathematical reasoning model named after the Bangla word for mathematics, Ganit, developed together with a new difficulty-aware Bengali math corpus and a curriculum-based GRPO pipeline.

## The Challenge and Solution

Bengali is one of the world's most widely spoken languages, yet existing LLMs either reason in English and then translate, or simply fail on multi-step Bengali math, in part because reinforcement learning recipes are tuned for high-resource languages and collapse under reward sparsity in low-resource settings.

To address this, the researchers constructed Ganit, a rigorously filtered and decontaminated Bengali math dataset with automatic difficulty tags derived from the pass@k of a strong evaluator model.

## Training Approach

Curriculum-GRPO combines multi-stage training (SFT + GRPO) with difficulty-aware sampling and verifiable rewards for format, numerical correctness, and Bengali reasoning.

## Key Results

On Bn-MGSM and Bn-MSVAMP benchmarks, GanitLLM-4B improves over its Qwen3-4B base by +8 and +7 accuracy points respectively, while increasing the percentage of Bengali reasoning tokens from 14% to over 88% and reducing average solution length from 943 to 193 words.

This work represents a significant advance in enabling large language models to reason natively in Bengali for mathematical problems rather than relying on translation.

## MCLM Benchmark

MCLM is a multilingual math benchmark featuring competition-level problems in 55 languages.

## Test-Time Scaling Methods

The research tests three test-time scaling methods—Outcome Reward Modeling (ORM), Process Reward Modeling (PRM), and Budget Forcing (BF)—on both Qwen2.5-1.5B Math and MR1-1.5B, a multilingual LLM trained for extended reasoning.

## Performance Results

Using Qwen2.5-1.5B Math with ORM achieves a score of 35.8 on MCLM, while BF on MR1-1.5B attains 35.2.

## Key Finding on Multilingual Generalization

While BF yields a 20-point improvement on English AIME, it provides only a 1.94-point average gain across other languages, and all tested methods fail to generalize robustly across languages. This suggests that test-time scaling methods, including budget forcing, are less effective at improving multilingual mathematical reasoning compared to their performance on English benchmarks.

Based on the web search results, here's what CaTS (Calibrated Test-Time Scaling) is about:

## Overview

CaTS adapts common repeated sampling methods, such as self-consistency and Best-of-N to handle queries of various difficulty.

## The Problem It Addresses

Best-of-N sampling and Self-Consistency with majority voting require a fixed number of sampling responses for each query, regardless of its complexity, which could result in wasted computation for simpler questions and insufficient exploration for more challenging ones.

## The Solution

The approach uses model confidence of responses for improving the efficiency of test-time scaling. However, LLMs are known to be overconfident and provide unreliable confidence estimation.

To tackle this, the method introduces Self-Calibration by distilling Self-Consistency-derived confidence into the model itself, enabling reliable confidence estimation at test time with one forward pass.

## Results

The approach proposes efficient test-time scaling by dynamically adjusting sampling strategies based on calibrated confidence scores, such as Early-Stopping for Best-of-N and Self-Consistency with calibrated confidence, with experiments showing that the approaches consistently outperform baselines under the same sample budget.

The research was presented at ICLR 2026 and addresses a key challenge in making LLM reasoning more efficient by adaptively allocating computational resources based on calibrated confidence estimates.

## Key Finding: Mixed Results Depending on Tuning Method

RL-tuned models generalize well across domains, while supervised fine-tuning (SFT)-tuned models often forget general capabilities. However, the overall picture is more nuanced.

## Domain Transfer Patterns

Most models that succeed in math fail to transfer their gains to other domains. When looking specifically at RL fine-tuning with math data, while RL post-training yields robust generalization improvements on in-domain mathematical tasks of varying difficulty, it shows negligible transfer to out-of-domain tasks.

## Why RL Differs from SFT

The research provides insights into the mechanism: SFT induces substantial representation and output drift, while RL preserves general-domain structure. Additionally, SFT tends to memorize training distributions, whereas RL can induce more transferable reasoning behavior.

## Broader Context

Some pioneering works focus on how to curate high-quality cross-domain datasets, including both synthetic and real-world questions into RL training to improve generalization across diverse reasoning tasks. This suggests that the training data composition matters significantly for achieving cross-domain transfer.

In summary, RL fine-tuning on math tasks shows better transfer potential than SFT, but still faces limitations in generalizing to out-of-domain tasks without explicit multi-domain training.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about training-free confidence estimation for LLMs using semantic entropy, self-consistency, and verbalized calibration:

## Key Approaches

Self-consistency generates multiple reasoning paths through temperature-based sampling and selects the most frequent answer by majority vote, implicitly using answer agreement as a confidence indicator.

Semantic entropy extends this idea by clustering semantically equivalent answers and computing entropy over the resulting distribution, providing a principled black-box uncertainty estimator that does not require access to model logits.

Common approaches to obtain confidence scores include token-level probabilities, semantic-level measures that evaluate agreement across multiple sampled completions, and explicitly verbalized percentages in a model's output.

## Verbalized Confidence vs. Semantic Entropy

Semantic Entropy leads to better calibrated scores than asking the model itself if the generated answer was correct, and recent work systematically compares verbalized confidence and semantic entropy under matched test-time compute budgets across several task domains.

## Recent Improvements

Confidence-Informed Self-Consistency (CISC) performs a weighted majority vote based on confidence scores obtained directly from the model, and by prioritizing high-confidence paths, it can identify the correct answer with a significantly smaller sample size.

So TigerLLM-1B is also built on Llama-3.2-1B, but with a significantly smaller Bengali corpus—just 10M tokens from educational texts compared to TituLLM's 37B tokens for their 1B/3B v2.0 models. This is a crucial distinction: both models share the same base architecture but diverge substantially in their training data scale.

This actually sets up a clean experimental design. I can isolate the effect of pretraining depth by comparing TigerLLM-1B and TituLLM-1B (same architecture and size, different corpus depth), and then isolate scale effects by comparing TituLLM-1B against TituLLM-3B (same architecture and training methodology, different model sizes). The TigerLLM-9B variant with Gemma-2 would add another dimension, though it introduces architectural variation.

I need to verify the exact token counts from the papers—TigerLLM used roughly 10M tokens for continual pretraining while TituLLM's corpus varies by version (v2.0 appears to be the 37B token variant mentioned in the ACL paper), but the magnitude difference is clear enough to support the comparison.

The corpus composition itself is interesting: TigerLLM's curated educational textbooks versus TituLLM's broad web crawl represents not just a depth difference but also a quality/curation axis that complicates the picture. The "Bengali Density" construct they're proposing (tokens per parameter) would help isolate the depth variable, but I should note that raw token count doesn't fully capture quality-adjusted depth—this is a confound worth flagging in the analysis.

For RQ2, I found a directly relevant paper on math reasoning transferability that shows RL-based approaches transfer better than SFT, and most models that excel at math fail to generalize elsewhere. Since the proposal uses SFT rather than RL, the literature suggests H2's "partial transfer" hypothesis might be too optimistic—the evidence points toward minimal transfer, which would actually make for a sharper, more falsifiable prediction.

I should recommend they measure transfer per domain (STEM-adjacent versus humanities) rather than in aggregate, grounding this in their own SFT/LIMO framing and the existing literature that predicts weak transfer.

Good — dropping LESS simplifies scope. Here's what the research turned up, and it hands you a much stronger fix for RQ1 than I expected, plus sharper, citable framing for RQ2 and RQ3.

## RQ1: the confound has a free fix already sitting on HuggingFace

The key discovery: **TigerLLM-1B and TituLLM-1B share the exact same base — Llama-3.2-1B** ([TigerLLM paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.10995), [TituLLM 1B checkpoint](https://huggingface.co/hishab/titulm-llama-3.2-1b-v1.1)). They differ enormously in Bengali pretraining depth: TigerLLM's continual pretraining corpus is ~10M tokens of curated Grade 6–12 textbooks, while TituLLM's v2.0 corpus is ~37B tokens of broad Bengali web text — roughly a 3,700x difference in raw depth, on identical architecture and identical parameter count. Both checkpoints are already public: [`md-nishat-008/TigerLLM-1B-it`](https://huggingface.co/md-nishat-008/TigerLLM-1B-it) and `hishab/titulm-llama-3.2-1b-v2.0`.

That means you can build two clean, single-variable comparisons instead of one confounded n=2 comparison, at zero extra pretraining cost:

- **Depth-isolated pair** (architecture and scale held fixed): TigerLLM-1B vs. TituLLM-1B. Both Llama-3.2-1B, both 1B params — the only thing that differs is Bengali pretraining depth. This is your real test of H1.
- **Scale-isolated pair** (architecture and pretraining methodology held fixed): TituLLM-1B vs. TituLLM-3B — both continual-pretrained on the same ~37B-token corpus, same pipeline, differing only in parameter count. This tests whether scale adds anything once depth is already saturated.
- **TigerLLM-9B** stays in as a supplementary/exploratory point (Gemma-2, different architecture) rather than part of the core causal claim — keep it, but label it explicitly as jointly varying architecture+scale+depth, not evidence for either H1 sub-claim alone.

Rewrite H1 as two precise, falsifiable sub-hypotheses instead of one blunt claim:
- **H1a (depth):** TituLLM-1B > TigerLLM-1B after identical LIMO fine-tuning, isolating depth from scale and architecture.
- **H1b (scale):** TituLLM-3B > TituLLM-1B, testing marginal returns to scale once depth is already deep.

One honest caveat to write into your validity-threats section: TigerLLM's corpus is small-but-curated (textbooks) while TituLLM's is large-but-broad (web crawl), so "depth" here is entangled with "curation quality," not pure token count. Don't bury this — turn it into a second finding. Report your "Bengali Density" (tokens/param) metric alongside a qualitative note on corpus curation, and frame the depth-isolated comparison as also testing TigerLLM's own thesis (small curated corpus > large generic scale) against TituLLM's brute-force approach. That's a second, citable contribution for free.

## RQ2: sharpen H2 using existing transfer literature, and use B-REASO's own metadata

[Does Math Reasoning Improve General LLM Capabilities? (arXiv 2507.00432)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.00432) found that RL-tuned models preserve general-domain structure and transfer reasonably, while **SFT-tuned models show representational drift and largely fail to transfer gains out-of-domain**. Your design is LIMO-style SFT, not RL — so the literature actually predicts weak-to-minimal transfer, not the generous "partial transfer" your current H2 states. Two changes:

1. **Sharpen H2**: predict minimal transfer under SFT, and explicitly connect it back to your problem statement's framing of GanitLLM's expensive RL pipeline. This turns RQ2 into a genuine cost-benefit argument: if cheap SFT elicits math gains but RL is needed for transfer, that's a real, decision-relevant finding for anyone choosing between the two approaches — which is exactly the practical question your problem statement opens with.
2. **Don't report one aggregate B-REASO delta.** B-REASO already tags questions by domain (STEM-adjacent vs. humanities/social science) and by difficulty tier (professional/college/high-school/middle-school). Break the transfer measurement down along both axes at no extra cost — this tells you whether any transfer is concentrated in STEM-adjacent reasoning items vs. rote-knowledge items, which is a much more diagnostic claim than a single number. It also lets you directly re-test TituLLM's own ACL finding that pretraining depth helped commonsense-style tasks but not Bangla MMLU-style broad knowledge — do the same split hold after reasoning fine-tuning? That ties RQ2 straight back to a specific claim in the literature you're already citing.

## RQ3: replace the single "untrained confidence" test with a 3-arm comparison

Verbalized self-report ("how sure are you?") is a known-weak signal — recent work directly comparing it to semantic entropy under matched compute budgets finds semantic entropy better calibrated (it clusters sampled answers by meaning and computes entropy over the cluster distribution, needs no logits or training). Recommend three arms instead of one:

- **Arm A — verbalized confidence** (your original plan): weak baseline, known to be unreliable in English; worth including specifically to demonstrate that.
- **Arm B — semantic entropy / self-consistency agreement rate** across k samples: a stronger training-free, black-box signal, still zero-training-cost, so it doesn't compromise your "cheap" framing.
- **Arm C — cited (not replicated) CaTS numbers** as an upper-bound reference point, explicitly labeled as not apples-to-apples, just context for how far training-free signals fall short of trained calibration.

This converts H3 from a vague "untrained confidence is imperfect" into a precise ranking prediction — semantic entropy/self-consistency > verbalized > fixed budget, trailing trained calibration — which is falsifiable and much harder for a reviewer to wave away.

One thing to check before committing to Arm B: semantic entropy's clustering step typically leans on an NLI/entailment model to judge answer equivalence, and Bengali-capable NLI models are thin on the ground. If you can't find one, you'd fall back to exact-answer-match clustering (weaker signal) or translate-then-cluster (introduces an English pivot you'd need to disclose as a limitation). Worth a quick check before you lock in the method — I can search for existing Bengali NLI/entailment models if you want that resolved now.

# XLSX creation, editing, and analysis

| Task | Approach |
|---|---|
| **Create** or **edit** with formulas/formatting | `openpyxl` — see gotchas below |
| **Bulk data** in or out | `pandas` (`read_excel`, `to_excel`) |
| **Quick look** at a sheet | `markitdown file.xlsx` — `## SheetName` per sheet; reads `.xlsm` too. No cell coordinates, so don't plan edits from it |
| **Read** a model (formulas *and* values) | two `load_workbook` passes — see gotchas |

> `openpyxl`, `pandas`, and `markitdown` are preinstalled — do not run `pip install` first; write the script and import directly. Only if an import fails (or the `markitdown` command is missing): `pip install` the missing package.

> Script paths below are relative to this skill's directory.

## Requirements for every output

- **Professional font** (Arial, Times New Roman) throughout, unless the user says otherwise.
- **Zero formula errors.** Never ship while `recalc.py` reports `errors_found`. If you think an error predates you, prove it: load the *original* with `data_only=True` and look at that cell. An error you introduced looks exactly like one you inherited.
- **Use formulas, never hardcoded results.** Write `sheet['B10'] = '=SUM(B2:B9)'`, not the Python-computed total. The sheet must recalculate when its inputs change.
- **Follow the user's spec literally.** Exact tab names, exact column headers, and the formula they spelled out. A redesign that computes something else fails, however elegant.
- **Document every assumption and hardcoded number** where the reader will see it — a cell comment, or an adjacent cell at a table's end. Cite a real source when one exists (`Source: Company 10-K, FY2024, Page 45, Revenue Note, [SEC EDGAR URL]`); when the number came from the user, say so plainly.
- **A workbook *you create* for someone to fill in** needs a short legend naming which cells to edit, and one example row of realistic values showing the expected format. Never add such a row to a file you were asked to edit.
- **Editing an existing file: match its conventions exactly.** They override every guideline here. Find its designated input cells first — a distinct font color, fill, or shading marks them — write only there, and leave every existing formula untouched.

## Recalculate (mandatory whenever the file contains formulas)

openpyxl writes formulas as strings with **no cached values**. Until you recalculate, every
formula cell reads back as `None` to anything reading cached values — `pandas`,
`load_workbook(data_only=True)`, and most previewers.

```bash
python scripts/recalc.py output.xlsx [timeout_seconds]   # default 30
```

LibreOffice computes every formula, the file is **rewritten in place**, and you get JSON:
`status` (`success` | `errors_found`), `total_formulas`, `total_errors`, and an
`error_summary` naming up to 100 cells per error type (`locations_truncated` says how many it
withheld — trust `total_errors`, not the length of the list). Fix what it names and run it
again. **JSON with an `error` key instead of a `status` means nothing was recalculated**, and
only that case exits non-zero — `errors_found` exits 0, so never treat a clean exit as a clean
workbook.

**A green recalc proves your formulas *evaluate*, not that they are *right*.** An off-by-one
range or a reference to the wrong row yields a clean, error-free file with wrong numbers.
Write 2–3 formulas first and check they pull the values you expect, before building out a grid.

**A workbook that links to another file loses those links** if you re-save it with openpyxl and
then recalculate. Such a formula reads `='[1]Returns Analysis'!$B$2` — the `[1]` is an index
into the workbook's external-reference list, naming a *separate file on disk*, not a sheet.
That file is rarely present here, so the cell's cached value is the only thing holding its
data. openpyxl strips that value on save; LibreOffice then has to resolve the reference for
real, fails, writes `#NAME?`, and deletes every link. `recalc.py` refuses to run in that state
— copy those cells' values out of the original before you save over them (`--force` overrides,
and accepts the loss).

## Choosing formulas that survive verification

LibreOffice implements fewer functions than Excel, and one it cannot evaluate becomes a
literal `#NAME?` baked into the file you deliver.

- **Prefer Excel-2007-era functions** — `SUMIFS`, `INDEX`, `MATCH`, `IFERROR`, `SUMPRODUCT` — which need no prefix.
- **Six post-2007 functions work, but only with an `_xlfn.` prefix**, because openpyxl writes your formula into the XML verbatim and Excel stores post-2007 names prefixed (its UI hides the prefix): `_xlfn.TEXTJOIN`, `_xlfn.CONCAT`, `_xlfn.IFS`, `_xlfn.SWITCH`, `_xlfn.MAXIFS`, `_xlfn.MINIFS`. Written bare, each yields `#NAME?`.
- **Never use `XLOOKUP`, `XMATCH`, `SORT`, `FILTER`, `UNIQUE`, or `SEQUENCE`.** The runtime's LibreOffice cannot evaluate them under *any* prefix. Newer builds do evaluate them, but they are spilling array functions and an openpyxl-written file has no spill metadata, so only the top-left cell of the range gets a value — and `recalc.py` reports `total_errors: 0` on the truncated result. Use `INDEX`/`MATCH` for lookups, and sort, filter, and de-duplicate in Python before writing the cells.
- A formula LibreOffice could not parse is written back **lowercased** — a quick tell beside a `#NAME?`.

## openpyxl gotchas

- **Reading a model takes two loads.** `data_only=True` yields cached values with the formulas gone; the default yields formula strings with no values. One pass cannot give you both.
- **`data_only=True` is destructive if you save.** That workbook has no formulas left, so saving replaces every one with a literal — permanently.
- **`data_only=True` on a file openpyxl just wrote returns `None` everywhere** — run `recalc.py` first. (A formula whose result is `""` also reads back as `None`.)
- **Merged cells: write the top-left anchor only.** Every other cell in the range is a `MergedCell` whose `.value` is read-only.
- **`.xlsm` loses its macros unless you pass `keep_vba=True`** to `load_workbook`.
- **A sheet name containing a space must be quoted** in a cross-sheet reference: `='Assumptions Inputs'!$B$5`. Unquoted, it evaluates to `#VALUE!`.

## Financial models

Unless the user says otherwise, or the existing file already does something else.

**Color:** blue text (`0,0,255`) for hardcoded inputs and scenario levers · black for formulas ·
green (`0,128,0`) for links to another sheet · red (`255,0,0`) for links to another file ·
yellow fill (`255,255,0`) for key assumptions and cells the user should fill in.

**Numbers:** currency `$#,##0`, with the unit named in the header (`Revenue ($mm)`) · zeros
render as `-`, including in percentages (`$#,##0;($#,##0);-`) · negatives in parentheses ·
percentages `0.0%`, **stored as fractions** (`0.15` renders `15.0%`; storing `15` renders
`1500.0%`) · valuation multiples `0.0x` · years as text (`"2024"`, never `2,024`).

**Structure:** every assumption in its own labeled cell, referenced by the formulas that use it
(`=B5*(1+$B$6)`, never `=B5*1.05`) · formulas consistent across every projection period, since a
lone edited cell mid-row is the commonest silent error · guard denominators that can be zero.

`openpyxl`, `pandas`, `markitdown` (pip, preinstalled — install only if an import fails or the command is missing) · LibreOffice (`soffice`, auto-configured for sandboxed environments via `scripts/office/soffice.py`)

aiTitle: Disentangling scale from pretraining depth in Bengali mathematical reasoning

content.thinking:
I've got a solid literature matrix with over 20 papers already reviewed and gaps clearly mapped out. One finding stands out for refining the approach: there's research on how constraining models to reason in a specific language affects accuracy, tested across the XReasoning benchmark with 370 parallel questions spanning 11 languages including Bengali.

The methodological precedent I'm seeing is particularly useful — they translated the LIMO dataset into Japanese, Thai, and Telugu for post-training experiments, which is exactly the kind of approach I'm considering, though Bengali remains notably absent from existing work. I also notice the LESS paper evaluates on TYDIQA which does include Bengali multilingual QA, and there's follow-up work on crosslingual reasoning through test-time scaling covering MGSM with 250 problems across 10 languages including Bengali. But here's a critical constraint for my research questions: models below 3B parameters don't benefit significantly from test-time scaling, which directly impacts how I should design the experiments around budget forcing and scaling benefits.

This is actually a key insight for the grid design — since TituLLM-1B and TigerLLM-1B are both sub-3B, the test-time confidence-based stopping mechanism in RQ3 might not show meaningful improvements at that scale. Rather than treating this as a blind spot, I should explicitly frame it as a testable extension: does this small-model scaling limitation replicate specifically in Bengali? The RQ1 grid comparing 1B depth-isolated pairs against 1B vs 3B scale pairs directly tests whether the existing finding about sub-3B models holds, and whether the constraint is about scale itself or about depth — which is exactly the differentiator the original problem emphasized.

I've also found practical dataset candidates: SOMADHAN and PatiGonit together provide around 19,000 Bengali math word problems that could serve as source pools for building the LIMO-style curated set rather than constructing from scratch. I should recommend subsampling from these combined with Ganit using LIMO's simplicity/difficulty criteria. There's also an output-language consistency risk flagged in the literature — models responding in English despite Bengali prompts — but that's already covered by the Bengali Language Adherence dependent variable in the P3 draft.

BenNumEval offers 3,255 natively-authored Bengali numerical reasoning samples across six tasks, which could strengthen the dependent variables for RQ1/RQ2 by adding a native-benchmark arm alongside the translated MGSM and MSVAMP versions, directly addressing the translation-bias validity threat already noted in the original proposal.

MetaFaith and Thought Calibration both highlight English-centric uncertainty expression gaps, while Kadavath's work explicitly flags the Bengali/LRL gap in their literature matrix—confirming this directly supports RQ3's novelty claim. Mathmatist presents another option with its 13-language benchmark including Bangla and 2,890 parallel Bangla-English gold QA pairs, offering additional native-benchmark coverage.

The parallel Bengali math benchmark is useful for RQ1/RQ2 evaluation, and its own gap notes about SFT improvements align perfectly with what this proposal tests. ## SOMADHAN Dataset

The SOMADHAN dataset is composed of 8,792 Bengali math word problems with intermediate reasoning steps and their corresponding answers. Currently, the dataset includes 4,000 manually annotated samples, each containing step-by-step reasoning and a final answer.

SOMADHAN focuses on complex Bengali math word problems and includes intermediate reasoning steps (chain of thought) for each solution, providing detailed, step-by-step logical reasoning, enabling models to learn and demonstrate multi-step problem-solving.

The dataset was created by utilizing the English GSM8K dataset as a foundation and employing expert human translators to manually translate the problems and solutions into Bengali, with the translation process following specific guidelines to preserve mathematical logic, contextual nuances, and cultural relevance.

The publicly available "PatiGonit" dataset from a Github repository contains equation-based simple MWPs. The PatiGonit dataset comprises 10,000 equation-based Bengali math word problems, containing a variation of simple and complex equations, where simple equations are defined as those containing only one mathematical operation, while complex equations involve multiple operations.

Both datasets address the need for Bengali language resources in mathematical reasoning, with SOMADHAN focusing on complex reasoning-based problems and PatiGonit focusing on equation-based problems.

**RQ1:** Does Bengali mathematical reasoning elicited by minimal-data (LIMO-style) fine-tuning depend more on model scale or on targeted Bengali pretraining depth, when architecture and depth-methodology confounds are controlled for?

**RQ2:** Does reasoning ability elicited through Bengali math fine-tuning transfer to non-math, high-stakes Bengali exam reasoning (B-REASO), and if so, is transfer concentrated in STEM-adjacent items or does it also reach broad-knowledge/humanities items?

**RQ3:** Can cheap, training-free confidence signals (verbalized self-report; semantic entropy / self-consistency agreement) support efficient test-time compute allocation in Bengali, and how do they rank against each other and against published trained-calibration (CaTS) numbers?

## P3 Hypotheses or Research Propositions

**H1a (depth, architecture+scale held fixed):** TituLLM-1B will outperform TigerLLM-1B after identical fine-tuning, because both share the Llama-3.2-1B base but TituLLM's pretraining corpus is ~3,700x larger (37B vs. ~10M Bengali tokens), isolating depth.

**H1b (scale, architecture+depth-methodology held fixed):** TituLLM-3B will outperform TituLLM-1B, but the margin will be smaller than the H1a margin — testing whether scale adds much once depth is already saturated. **H2 (transfer, sharpened from "partial" using arXiv 2507.00432 — SFT preserves less general structure than RL):** Because our elicitation method is SFT (not RL, unlike GanitLLM), we expect *minimal* transfer to non-math B-REASO domains overall, with what transfer does occur concentrated in STEM-adjacent/professional-tier items rather than humanities or middle-school-tier items — directly re-testing TituLLM's own finding that its pretraining depth helped commonsense-style tasks but not Bangla-MMLU-style broad knowledge.

**H3 (confidence ranking):** Training-free signals will rank semantic entropy/self-consistency agreement > verbalized self-report > fixed budget, in both accuracy-per-token efficiency and calibration error, but all will fall short of CaTS's published trained-calibration numbers (cited as an upper-bound reference, not replicated).

**Independent variables:** backbone identity (TigerLLM-1B, TituLLM-1B, TituLLM-3B, TigerLLM-9B); Bengali pretraining depth (operationalized as Bengali Density = pretraining tokens / parameter count, plus a qualitative curated-vs-broad-corpus label); model scale (1B/3B/9B); fine-tuning data (identical 1,000-example LIMO-style Bengali set across all backbones); test-time compute-allocation policy (fixed budget vs. verbalized-confidence stopping vs. semantic-entropy/self-consistency stopping).

content.thinking:
The user is asking three specific things: whether TigerLLM's 10M tokens counts as actual pretraining or just fine-tuning (and what the terminology distinction is), whether this work is feasible on a single RTX 5060 Ti with 16GB VRAM, and how to handle the practical challenge of frequent power outages through checkpointing and backup strategies. I need to give precise, grounded answers to each of these concerns.

So on the terminology question — the paper itself calls the 10M token stage "continual pretraining" (sometimes written as "continued pretraining"), which is distinct from both full pretraining from scratch and standard instruction fine-tuning. Continual pretraining means taking an already-pretrained model like LLaMA 3.2 and continuing the next-token prediction objective on new raw text data to inject domain-specific knowledge, whereas full pretraining would start from random weights and require trillions of tokens. The TigerLLM approach then follows this with instruction-tuning on 100K QA pairs, which is the supervised fine-tuning stage. ive pretraining (DAPT): taking existing pretrained weights and continuing the unsupervised language modeling objective on new domain- or language-specific raw text — both TigerLLM (10M tokens) and TituLLM (37B tokens) do this to inject Bengali. Fine-tuning or instruction-tuning (SFT) is the supervised stage on labeled (input, output) pairs — like TigerLLM's 100K Bangla-Instruct pairs or the reasoning elicitation in the study itself. So TigerLLM's Bengali depth comes from continual pretraining rather than full pretraining or just fine-tuning, but 10M tokens is an extremely light dose — practically straddling the line between continued pretraining and heavy fine-tuning, which is worth flagging explicitly.

The Bengali Density metric really highlights this: TigerLLM-1B gets roughly 0.01 tokens/param versus TituLLM-1B's 37 tokens/param — a roughly 3,700x difference. I should be more precise in the write-up and describe TigerLLM's stage as "light continual pretraining" or "domain-adaptive pretraining" rather than treating it as equivalent to TituLLM's broader continual pretraining, even though I already flagged the curated-versus-broad distinction. Now I'm thinking through the hardware feasibility question for an RTX 5060 Ti with 16GB VRAM.

For fine-tuning these models, LoRA and QLoRA are very feasible across all three — TigerLLM-1B, TituLLM-1B, and TituLLM-3B. Full fine-tuning of the 1B models in bf16 is also workable since the weights alone take about 2GB, and with Adam optimizer states that's roughly 16-20GB total, which is borderline but LoRA fits comfortably. The 3B model is tighter for full fine-tuning — 6GB for weights plus optimizer states pushes toward 24GB total, which exceeds the 16GB limit, so LoRA is the better choice there.

TigerLLM-9B is the real constraint. Full fine-tuning isn't feasible on 16GB since it would need 100GB+ for Adam in fp32 or at least 36GB+ even in pure bf16 without quantization. However, QLoRA with 4-bit quantization of the base model plus LoRA adapters can fit a 9B model on 16GB VRAM — this is actually the intended use case for QLoRA.

Fine-tuning the 9B model on a 5060 Ti would be tight but doable with careful management: batch size of 1-2, gradient checkpointing, shorter sequences, and gradient accumulation. Inference and evaluation at 9B in 4-bit or 8-bit quantization is very feasible on 16GB.

The real bottleneck for the evaluation loops (budget forcing, multiple samples for self-consistency, semantic entropy) isn't VRAM but throughput — generating many samples per question takes time on a single consumer GPU.

Generating k=5-10 samples per question across multiple benchmarks (250+3255+13497+10544 items) with multiple backbones and conditions means a lot of generation calls that could take many hours to days, especially for the 9B model with long reasoning traces. I should plan to subsample benchmarks strategically — using official test subsets or stratified samples rather than the full 13,497 items from B-REASO — to keep this within feasible time.

LIMO-style fine-tuning is designed to be cheap (a few hundred to a thousand examples, short training), which aligns well with consumer hardware constraints, unlike some other approaches.

content.text:
**TigerLLM: continual pretraining, not full pretraining, and not ordinary fine-tuning.** The paper's own terminology is "continual pretraining" (also called continued/domain-adaptive pretraining): it takes the already-pretrained Llama-3.2-1B/Gemma-2-9B weights and continues the plain next-token-prediction objective on raw, unlabeled Bengali text (the 10M-token textbook corpus) — no instruction format, no task labels. That's a different thing from full pretraining (training from random initialization on trillions of tokens) and different from fine-tuning/SFT (supervised (input, output) pairs — that's the separate Bangla-Instruct 100K-pair stage they do afterward).

Your instinct is right to flag it, though: 10M tokens is an extremely light dose for something called "pretraining." Continual-pretraining papers typically use billions of tokens; TituLLM's is 37B. So TigerLLM-1B sits at roughly 0.01 tokens/param of Bengali depth versus TituLLM-1B's ~37 tokens/param — a ~3,700x gap, which is exactly the axis your depth-isolated comparison (H1a) is testing. This is worth stating precisely in your methods section rather than just saying "pretraining depth" — call it "continual-pretraining token count," since that's the accurate construct.

**Hardware: your 5060 Ti 16GB can run this whole study, with one adjustment.** Use LoRA/QLoRA uniformly across all four backbones rather than full fine-tuning:

- TigerLLM-1B, TituLLM-1B, TituLLM-3B: comfortable with LoRA in bf16 on 16GB, fast — LIMO-style runs (1,000 examples, a handful of epochs) should take well under an hour each.
- TigerLLM-9B: full fine-tuning won't fit (Adam optimizer states alone need 30GB+), but QLoRA (4-bit quantized base + LoRA adapters) is exactly what 16GB cards are used for at this scale — feasible with gradient checkpointing and small batch size, just slower.

Using LoRA/QLoRA for every backbone isn't just a hardware workaround — it keeps the elicitation method identical across all four models, which matters for RQ1's causal claim, and it's actually more consistent with LIMO's own "cheap, lightweight post-training" philosophy than full fine-tuning would be. Worth stating explicitly in your methods as a deliberate choice, not just a constraint.

The real time sink isn't fine-tuning — it's RQ3's multi-sample generation (self-consistency/semantic entropy need k samples per question) run across large benchmarks. Running that at full scale (B-REASO's 13,497 items × 4 backbones × multiple conditions) on one consumer GPU would take a long time. I'd scope that down: use a stratified subsample of B-REASO (e.g., ~1,000–1,500 items, stratified by domain and difficulty tier so the breakdown in RQ2 still works) as your primary evaluation set, and note the full set as available for a supplementary run if time allows.

**Electricity reliability — this is a real risk to engineer around, not just note:**
- Make every training and eval script checkpoint/resume-safe: save LoRA adapter checkpoints every N steps, and for eval loops, write each result to disk (append to JSONL) immediately after it's generated rather than holding results in memory — a power cut then loses at most the last unflushed item, not the run.
- A small UPS (even 600–1000VA) buys 10–20 minutes, enough to trigger a graceful save-and-stop on outage — worth the modest cost given how much repeated-run time it'd save over a semester.
- Keep a cloud fallback in your back pocket for the 9B QLoRA runs and the large multi-sample RQ3 passes specifically (Colab/Kaggle free tiers, or your university's GPU cluster if the department has one) — reserve local compute for the cheaper 1B/3B LoRA runs and smaller eval passes, and burst to cloud only for the parts most vulnerable to a multi-hour outage.

Here's the whole form rewritten in plain language — same rigor underneath, but said the way a person would say it. Everything is still specific enough for a reviewer (real model names, real token counts, real statistical tests), just without the dense phrasing.

---

## P3 Draft Research Questions

**RQ1.** When we give a model a small set of Bengali math examples to "wake up" its reasoning, what actually decides whether it works — how big the model is, or how much Bengali it saw during its original training? We compare models that differ in only one of those two things at a time, so we can tell them apart instead of guessing.

**RQ2.** If a model gets better at Bengali math after this training, does that thinking ability carry over to non-math questions? We test it on B-REASO, a Bengali exam-style benchmark covering 50 subjects, and check whether any improvement shows up across the board or only in science-type subjects.

**RQ3.** Can a model tell when it's confident enough to stop thinking, without us paying to train it for that? We try two cheap ways of reading its confidence and see whether either one saves computation without hurting accuracy.

---

## P3 Hypotheses or Research Propositions

**H1a — Bengali depth matters more than size.** TituLLM-1B should beat TigerLLM-1B after both get the exact same training. This is a fair fight: both are built on the same Llama-3.2-1B base and both have 1 billion parameters. The only real difference is that TituLLM continued training on about 37 billion Bengali tokens while TigerLLM used about 10 million — roughly 3,700 times more Bengali exposure. If TituLLM wins, Bengali depth is doing the work, not size or architecture.

**H1b — Size helps, but less than depth.** TituLLM-3B should beat TituLLM-1B, since it's bigger, but by a smaller margin than the gap in H1a. Both were trained the same way on the same corpus, so size is the only thing changing. There's a specific reason to watch the 1B→3B step closely: earlier cross-lingual work found that models under 3B parameters barely benefit from test-time scaling. That was tested on general multilingual models, never on models built specifically for Bengali. If that finding holds here too, we should see a noticeable jump right at that step.

**H2 — Transfer will be weak, and unevenly spread.** We expect the math gains to mostly stay in math. Recent work found that supervised fine-tuning (what we're doing) tends to shift a model's behavior toward the training data and doesn't carry over to new domains, while reinforcement learning holds onto general ability better. Since GanitLLM used reinforcement learning and we're deliberately using the cheap supervised route, we predict little transfer overall — and whatever transfer does appear should show up in science-type B-REASO subjects rather than humanities. This also lets us re-check something TituLLM found about itself: its Bengali training helped on commonsense tasks but did nothing for broad knowledge tasks. We can see whether that same split survives after reasoning training.

**H3 — Free confidence signals will help a little, but won't match trained ones.** We expect the ranking to be: sampling the model several times and measuring how much its answers agree (semantic entropy) works best, simply asking it "how sure are you?" works worse, and a fixed thinking budget works worst. All three should fall short of CaTS, which spent real money training a model to judge its own confidence. We cite CaTS's published numbers as a reference point — we are not re-running their pipeline.

---

## P3 Variables, Constructs, or Key Concepts

**What we change (independent variables):**
- Which model we start from — TigerLLM-1B, TituLLM-1B, TituLLM-3B, and TigerLLM-9B.
- How much Bengali that model saw during its original training. We measure this as "Bengali Density" — pretraining tokens divided by parameter count — and we also label whether the corpus was small-and-curated or large-and-broad, because those aren't the same kind of depth.
- Model size — 1B, 3B, or 9B parameters.
- How the model decides when to stop thinking — a fixed budget, its own spoken confidence, or agreement across multiple samples.

**What stays fixed:** every model gets the identical 1,000-example Bengali math set, trained the same way with the same settings. That's what makes the comparison fair.

**What we measure (dependent variables):**
- Accuracy on Bengali math benchmarks (Bn-MGSM, GSM-Plus-BN, BenNumEval).
- Accuracy on B-REASO, reported both overall and split by subject area and by difficulty level.
- Whether the model actually thinks in Bengali or drifts into English mid-reasoning — we report this as a percentage of reasoning tokens that stay in Bengali.
- How many thinking tokens each answer costs, so we can compare accuracy against computation spent.
- How well the model's confidence lines up with whether it was actually right.

**Core ideas:** reasoning elicitation (waking up ability the model already has rather than teaching it from scratch); targeted pretraining depth versus raw scale; test-time compute; calibration; and whether reasoning transfers across domains.

---

## P3 Planned Study or Evaluation Design

- **Controlled experiment** — we keep the training data and method identical and change only the starting model, one variable at a time.
- **Model design and evaluation** — we apply the same lightweight fine-tuning to four models and build a custom loop that controls how long each one thinks.
- **NLP experiment** — we look at language behavior, mainly whether the model stays in Bengali while reasoning.
- **Benchmarking or performance evaluation** — we test against both translated and originally-Bengali benchmarks.

---

## P3 RQ to Method Alignment

**RQ1.** We fine-tune all four models on the exact same 1,000 Bengali math problems, using the same method and settings. Then we make two clean comparisons. TigerLLM-1B versus TituLLM-1B isolates Bengali depth, because everything else — base model, architecture, parameter count — is identical. TituLLM-1B versus TituLLM-3B isolates size, because both came from the same corpus and the same training pipeline. TigerLLM-9B is included as an extra data point, but we say openly that it differs in architecture, size, *and* depth all at once, so we don't use it to support either hypothesis. This is the fix for the most obvious hole a reviewer would poke: comparing just two models that differ in three ways proves nothing.

**RQ2.** We take those same fine-tuned models and run them on B-REASO without any further training. Then we compare how much they improved on math against how much they improved on exams. Crucially, we don't report one averaged number — B-REASO already tags every question by subject and by difficulty level, so we break the results down along both. That tells us not just *whether* reasoning transferred but *where*, which is a far more useful finding.

**RQ3.** We run the fine-tuned models three ways on the math benchmarks: with a fixed thinking budget, with the model stopping when it says it's confident, and with the model stopping when repeated samples agree with each other. We compare accuracy against thinking tokens spent for each, and we place the results next to CaTS's published numbers to show how far a free method gets you compared to a paid one.

---

## P3 Validity Threats and Mitigation Plan

**Mixed-up causes (confounding).** TigerLLM-9B differs from the others in several ways at once, so any result involving it can't tell us which difference caused what. We handle this by keeping it out of our main claims entirely and reporting it only as an exploratory extra.

**Are we really measuring "depth"? (construct validity).** This is the honest weak point. TigerLLM's 10 million tokens are carefully curated school textbooks; TituLLM's 37 billion are broad web text. So "more tokens" is tangled up with "different kind of text." Rather than hide this, we make it a second finding: we report Bengali Density alongside a note on what kind of corpus each model used, and we frame the comparison as also testing small-but-curated versus large-but-broad. That's a real question in its own right, and TigerLLM's own paper argues the curated side.

**Translation bias in the data.** Some benchmarks (Bn-MGSM, GSM-Plus-BN) are translated from English, which might quietly favor models with more English training. We report those separately from BenNumEval and B-REASO, which were written in Bengali originally, so any translation advantage becomes visible instead of hidden in an average.

**Small samples.** Some benchmarks are small — Bn-MGSM has only 250 problems — so a few lucky answers can look like a real difference. We report bootstrap confidence intervals rather than bare accuracy numbers, and use a paired test (McNemar's) for our two key comparisons, since every model answers the same questions.

**Only four models.** Four starting points is not a full grid. We describe our findings as directional evidence for these specific model families, not a universal law about scale versus depth.

**Bugs in our own code.** Custom thinking-loops are easy to get subtly wrong. We build ours on top of the published BatsResearch cross-lingual test-time scaling codebase rather than writing it from scratch, and we manually read through about 50 reasoning traces per model per setting to catch the model looping, repeating itself, or producing fluent nonsense.

**Does this generalize?** Our results apply to the Llama-3.2 and Gemma-2 families and to Bengali specifically. We won't claim they hold for other architectures or other low-resource languages without someone testing that.

---

## Group Number

*I still need this from you — write your assigned number here.*

---

## P4 Selected Methods

Controlled experiment; Model design and evaluation; NLP experiment; Benchmarking or performance evaluation.

---

## P4 Data, Participants, System, Benchmark, or Repository Details

**No human participants.** This is entirely a computational study using publicly released models and datasets.

**The four models we start from.** TigerLLM-1B (built on Llama-3.2-1B, then continued training on roughly 10 million tokens of curated Bangla school textbooks), TituLLM-1B and TituLLM-3B (both built on Llama-3.2 and continued on the same roughly 37-billion-token broad Bengali corpus), and TigerLLM-9B (built on Gemma-2-9B, included as a supplementary point). All four are already public, so we don't train anything from scratch.

**The training set.** We build one set of 1,000 high-quality Bengali math problems with worked solutions, drawn from three existing collections: GanitLLM's GANIT training pool (which already comes with difficulty labels), SOMADHAN (8,792 complex Bengali word problems with human-written step-by-step solutions), and PatiGonit (10,000 equation-style Bengali problems). We select from these using the same kind of quality-and-difficulty filtering LIMO and s1 used. Every model gets this identical set — that's the whole point.

**What we test on.** Bn-MGSM (250 translated problems), GSM-Plus-BN (10,544 items built by perturbing 1,318 seed questions, translation checked by humans), BenNumEval (3,255 originally-Bengali numerical reasoning items across six task types), and B-REASO (13,497 originally-Bengali multiple-choice questions spanning 50 subjects and four difficulty levels), plus its harder B-REASO HEAVY subset.

**Our computing setup.** A single NVIDIA RTX 5060 Ti with 16GB of memory. Because of this, we use LoRA for the smaller models and QLoRA (4-bit) for the 9B model rather than full fine-tuning. This is a deliberate choice, not just a workaround — it keeps the training method identical across all four models, which our comparison depends on, and it fits LIMO's own argument that reasoning can be elicited cheaply. For B-REASO, we evaluate on a stratified sample of roughly 1,000–1,500 questions, chosen to preserve the subject and difficulty mix so our RQ2 breakdown still works, with the full set reserved for a supplementary run if time permits.

---

## P4 Instrument, Dataset, Repository, Prototype, or Benchmark Link

**Models (all confirmed available):**
- TigerLLM-1B: https://huggingface.co/md-nishat-008/TigerLLM-1B-it
- TigerLLM-9B: https://huggingface.co/md-nishat-008/TigerLLM-9B-it
- TituLLM-1B: https://huggingface.co/hishab/titulm-llama-3.2-1b-v1.1
- TituLLM-3B: https://huggingface.co/hishab/titulm-llama-3.2-3b-v1.1

**Datasets:**
- SOMADHAN: https://data.mendeley.com/datasets/34bs5cxk9j/2 (confirmed)
- PatiGonit: N/A — public repo referenced inside https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.21354; exact URL to be pulled from that paper.
- GANIT (GanitLLM): N/A — described in https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.06767; repository link not yet located.
- GSM-Plus-BN: N/A — described in https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.13248; repository link not yet located.
- BenNumEval: N/A — described in https://aclanthology.org/2025.findings-acl.915.pdf; repository link not yet located.
- B-REASO: N/A — described in https://aclanthology.org/2025.findings-emnlp.492/; repository link not yet located.

**Code we build on:**
- Budget-forcing reference implementation: https://github.com/BatsResearch/crosslingual-test-time-scaling
- CaTS (cited for comparison only, not re-run): https://openreview.net/forum?id=jrSc4RJXy1

---

**H1a — Bengali depth matters more than size.** TituLLM-1B should beat TigerLLM-1B after both get identical training. This is a genuinely fair fight: both are built on the same Llama-3.2-1B base, both have 1 billion parameters, both use the same architecture. The only meaningful difference is that TituLLM continued training on about 37 billion Bengali tokens while TigerLLM used about 10 million — roughly 3,700 times more Bengali exposure. If TituLLM wins, depth is doing the work and we can say so cleanly.

**H1b — More parameters won't automatically help, because the same corpus gets spread thinner.** This one is more interesting than it first looks. TituLLM-1B and TituLLM-3B were trained on the *same* 37-billion-token corpus. That means the 1B model saw about 37 tokens of Bengali per parameter, while the 3B model saw only about 12 — the bigger model is actually *less* saturated in Bengali per unit of capacity. So this isn't a simple "bigger wins" prediction. If raw size is what matters, the 3B wins. If how thoroughly the Bengali soaked in is what matters, the 1B could hold its own or even win. Based on the search results, I found detailed information about the s1K curation methodology. Here's what the research shows:

## s1K Dataset Curation Methodology

The s1K dataset was created by filtering from a pool of 59,000 questions using three stages of filtering based on three guiding principles: Quality, Difficulty, and Diversity, to arrive at a minimal set of 1,000 samples.

### Quality Filtering

Quality filtering first removes questions with API errors (reducing the dataset to 54,116 samples), then filters out low-quality examples containing formatting issues like ASCII art diagrams, non-existent image references, or inconsistent question numbering (reducing to 51,581 examples).

### Difficulty Filtering

For difficulty, two indicators are used: model performance and reasoning trace length. Two models (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct) are evaluated on each question, with correctness assessed by Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and token length of reasoning traces is measured using the Qwen2.5 tokenizer. Questions that either model can solve correctly are removed as they may be too easy.

### Diversity Filtering

The diversity stage aims to ensure broad coverage and balanced complexity in the selected data by combining manual curation with domain-stratified sampling. 384 samples are identified for the final 1,000 samples from datasets perceived as high-quality and not in need of further filtering.

The dataset consists of 1,000 questions paired with reasoning traces.

Based on the search results, here's comprehensive information about LIMO's 817 examples curation criteria and reasoning chain quality:

## Overview

LIMO demonstrates that complex mathematical reasoning can be effectively elicited with a significantly reduced number of training instances, specifically only 817 carefully curated examples.

## Curation Criteria

The curation process included defining selection criteria based on complexity, knowledge diversity, and deviation from the model's training distribution. More specifically:

**Difficulty Selection:** Problems are filtered using state-of-the-art models (e.g., Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct), retaining only those with <10% solve rates. Problems that this model solved correctly within four attempts were excluded, ensuring that only non-trivial problems remained.

**Diversity:** Selected from advanced benchmarks (AIME, OlympiadBench) and multilingual sources (Chinese Gaokao), ensuring coverage of algebra, geometry, and proof-based challenges. Additionally, strategic sampling techniques balanced representation across mathematical domains and complexity levels while avoiding conceptual redundancy.

**Out-of-Distribution Focus:** 30% of questions intentionally deviate from standard datasets to test generalization.

## Reasoning Chain Quality

The underlying idea is to induce the model to integrate meta-reasoning into a cohesive reasoning chain through these narrow yet focused training examples. The Less-Is-More Reasoning Hypothesis proposes that sophisticated reasoning capabilities can emerge through minimal but precisely orchestrated demonstrations of cognitive processes.

## Results

With merely 817 curated training samples, LIMO improves the performance of previous strong SFT-based models from 6.5% to 57.1% on AIME and from 59.2% to 94.8% on MATH, while only using 1% of the training data required by previous approaches.

Based on the search results, here's what I found on this topic:

## Key Research Areas

The search results reveal several recent approaches to multilingual reasoning distillation and translating reasoning traces for low-resource languages:

### Challenges with Translated Reasoning Traces

Machine translation can introduce noise and is prone to inconsistencies or errors in mathematical expressions, quantities, and logical dependencies, and translated reasoning traces may not match the model's own reasoning behavior, causing train-inference distribution mismatch.

### Supervised Fine-Tuning Limitations

SFT on distilled multilingual traces improves language consistency, but the quality and scale of supervised multilingual reasoning data limit its gains, and SFT can introduce severe repetition issues in some languages.

### Alternative Approaches

Recent work includes:

- **Crosslingual On-Policy Self-Distillation (COPSD)**: This approach transfers a model's own high-resource reasoning behavior to low-resource languages, using the same model as student and teacher where the student sees only the low-resource problem while the teacher receives privileged crosslingual context, and training minimizes full-distribution token-level divergence on the student's own rollouts.

- **Linguistic Reasoning Traces for Machine Translation**: Linguistic reasoning traces are most effective when used as in-context guidance, but using them as training data yields smaller and less consistent gains as models can learn to reproduce the trace format but still often generate imperfect reasoning content.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about the research on controlling thinking language in multilingual reasoning models:

## "When Models Reason in Your Language" Research

The study uses post-training on Distilled-R1-7B with mini training sets of 100, 250, 500, and 817 instances per low-resource language (Japanese, Thai, Telugu).

### LIMO Dataset

The training data are filtered from LIMO (Ye et al., 2025), comprising math problems with step-by-step solutions from the teacher model (DeepSeek-R1-671B), and translated by GPT-4o-mini.

### Key Findings

The research examines language matching rate and answer accuracy of Distilled-R1-7B with no post-training and with post-training on 100 and 250 instances for the three languages: Japanese, Thai, and Telugu. The study illustrates changes in language matching and answer accuracy before and after post-training when the models are prompted to think in Japanese, Thai, or Telugu.

The full paper is titled "When Models Reason in Your Language: Controlling Thinking Language Comes at the Cost of Accuracy" and explores the tradeoffs between controlling the language models use for reasoning and maintaining their accuracy.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about GanitLLM and the GANIT dataset:

## Overview

GanitLLM is a Bengali mathematical reasoning model presented together with a new difficulty-aware Bengali math corpus and a curriculum-based GRPO pipeline.

## Dataset Construction

Starting from approximately 1.5M Bengali math problems, the GANIT dataset applies multi-stage quality filtration, verification, deduplication, and decontamination to obtain GANIT-TRAIN and GANIT-DEV. 

The GANIT dataset is a rigorously filtered and decontaminated Bengali math dataset with automatic difficulty tags derived from the pass@k of a strong evaluator model.

## Reasoning Traces Construction

Much of the reasoning-related pretraining data is in English, often with long reasoning traces. The dataset construction addressed this by grounding the model's reasoning in Bengali through step-by-step chain-of-thought annotated solutions, reducing reliance on translation and code-switching.

## Training Approach

The Curriculum-GRPO approach combines multi-stage training (SFT + GRPO) with difficulty-aware sampling and verifiable rewards for format, numerical correctness, and Bengali reasoning.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about benchmark decontamination using n-gram overlap as a standard practice for LLMs:

## Standard Practice Established by GPT-3

The GPT-3 family established n-gram-based decontamination as a standard pre-training practice, and it has become widely adopted in the field.

## N-gram Overlap Methodology

The decontamination method involves computing n-gram Jaccard similarity between train and test documents, typically using 13-grams, and removing train documents that have a Jaccard similarity over 0.8. OpenAI defined a test document as contaminated if any N-gram overlap existed with any training document, using a range of N values between 8 and 13 depending on dataset.

## Implementation Details

The decontamination pipeline constructs n-gram representations of downstream task datasets and removes any matching content from the training corpus by extracting n-grams of size 8–13 from the test split (or validation split).

## Limitations and Evolving Approaches

However, it's important to note that models trained on rephrased test sets can reach high accuracy while being undetectable by n-gram overlap, indicating that this method alone has limitations. Recent work emphasizes that contamination is difficult to define uniformly and that its impact depends on task, model, and training recipe.

content.thinking:
GANIT already has the infrastructure in place—multi-stage quality filtering, verification, deduplication, decontamination, and automatic difficulty tags based on evaluator performance. What's particularly valuable is that GANIT-TRAIN includes Bengali step-by-step CoT annotated solutions with a built-in CoT-SFT split, which means they don't need to construct this from scratch but can instead focus on selecting the right data from what's already available.

This is a massive de-risking move. There's a potential circularity concern if they're comparing against GanitLLM while drawing from GANIT, but actually it's the opposite—it's a strength. They'd be using the exact same data pool as GanitLLM but with LIMO-style minimal selection and cheap SFT instead of expensive curriculum-GRPO. That's a controlled comparison: same data source, different training paradigm. They can make a direct claim that GanitLLM used costly RL on this pool while they achieve results with just 1,000 examples via SFT. The caveat is that GanitLLM used Qwen3-4B as the backbone while they might use something different, so it's not perfectly controlled, but holding the data source constant is still meaningful.

Both approaches rely on a strong model's failures to signal difficulty, but in Bengali that conflates math difficulty with comprehension difficulty—a problem might look "hard" only because the model can't parse the language, not because the math is actually hard. This is actually a mini-version of their core research question about whether English-derived data-selection criteria work in Bengali, which connects back to the LESS thread they cut earlier. That's worth flagging as a methodological trap central to what they're investigating.

For the actual filtering approach, I'm weighing three options: filtering on Bengali versions directly (conflates linguistic and math difficulty), filtering on English source problems where parallels exist (cleaner math difficulty signal), or using GANIT's existing pass@k tags (free and already computed, but the evaluator model's Bengali ability is unknown). The cleanest path forward is leveraging GANIT's tags as primary but validating against English-parallel difficulty where available—SOMADHAN is derived from GSM8K, so English parallels exist there. Better yet, report difficulty two ways and check if Bengali-derived and English-derived rankings correlate; if they diverge significantly, that's itself a finding worth reporting.

Now looking at the trace sources: SOMADHAN has human-written step-by-step solutions in Bengali (4,000 manually annotated), which is rarer and higher quality than translated traces. GANIT also has Bengali CoT-annotated solutions in its CoT-SFT split. PatiGonit is equation-based and simple—probably too easy for LIMO-style work, which targets hard problems.

I need to correct my earlier recommendation: PatiGonit shouldn't be a primary training source since simple one-operation equations are exactly what LIMO's difficulty filter would reject. It's better positioned as a calibration set for easy problems rather than core training data.

There's also the trace length issue—s1 used reasoning trace length as a difficulty signal, but Bengali's lower token efficiency means English length thresholds won't transfer directly, so I'll need to normalize for that.

Now I'm spotting a critical data contamination problem. Their evaluation sets all trace back to GSM8K: SOMADHAN was created by translating GSM8K into Bengali, Bn-MGSM is a Bengali translation of GSM8K, and GSM-Plus-BN is a perturbed version of GSM8K. If they're training on SOMADHAN and evaluating on the other two, that's massive contamination across all three benchmarks. The real issue is that standard n-gram decontamination won't catch this—two different Bengali translations of the same underlying GSM8K problem would have completely different surface text but represent identical problems. What they actually need is source-level decontamination that matches against the original English problem IDs, not just string similarity on the Bengali side. This is a concrete, actionable fix that could meaningfully strengthen their methodology.
