I should also note what to drop from PatiGonit and identify an ablation opportunity around dataset size—testing 100/250/500/1000 examples would give them a data-efficiency curve that's much stronger than just picking 1000 arbitrarily.

The tradeoff is real though: varying size across three models means 12 total training runs, but on 1B/3B LoRA that's still manageable in 30-90 minutes each, so maybe 2-3 sizes is the practical sweet spot. I'll write this up in plain language, being clear about what's established practice versus what I'm recommending, keeping it organized and substantial without padding.

content.text:
Researched it properly. Here's what I found, and there's one serious problem in the plan I gave you earlier that needs fixing before anything else.

## First: the contamination trap that could sink your results

Trace where your data actually comes from:

- **SOMADHAN** was built by taking English **GSM8K** and having human translators render it into Bengali.
- **Bn-MGSM** is 250 problems from **GSM8K**, manually translated.
- **GSM-Plus-BN** is built by perturbing 1,318 seed questions from **GSM-Plus**, which itself is built from **GSM8K**.

All three trace back to the same English source. If you train on SOMADHAN and test on Bn-MGSM or GSM-Plus-BN, you may be testing on problems your model already saw — just wearing different clothes.

Worse, **standard decontamination won't catch this.** The usual practice is n-gram overlap (typically 13-grams, Jaccard similarity above 0.8), which compares surface text. But two independent Bengali translations of the same GSM8K problem will share almost no n-grams while being the *identical problem*. Your decontamination check would come back clean and you'd never know.

**What you have to do instead:** decontaminate at the level of the underlying English source problem, not the Bengali string. Concretely — for every candidate training item, trace it back to its GSM8K ID (or its English source text), and exclude anything whose English ancestor appears in the GSM8K test split, in MGSM's 250, or in GSM-Plus's 1,318 seeds. Only after that ID-level pass do you run normal n-gram checking as a second net. Write this into the paper explicitly; reviewers in multilingual NLP are increasingly alert to exactly this failure, and being the paper that handled it properly is a small credibility win.

If SOMADHAN turns out to draw from the GSM8K *test* split rather than train, you may need to drop it as a training source entirely and lean on GANIT. Check this in Week 1 — it's a go/no-go item.

## Second: GANIT already did most of your work

Reading GanitLLM's construction more closely, the GANIT dataset was built from ~1.5M Bengali math problems and already went through multi-stage quality filtration, verification, deduplication, and decontamination, and it carries **automatic difficulty tags derived from pass@k of a strong evaluator model**. It also has a **CoT-SFT split** with Bengali step-by-step solutions — the authors specifically grounded reasoning in Bengali to reduce translation and code-switching.

That's exactly the raw material LIMO-style curation needs, already cleaned. Your job shrinks from "build a dataset" to "select 1,000 items from a curated pool" — which is what LIMO actually is anyway.

It also hands you a stronger comparison than you had. GanitLLM used expensive curriculum-GRPO on this pool; you'd be using 1,000 examples and cheap SFT **from the same pool**. Holding the data source constant while varying only the training paradigm makes your cost-benefit argument much sharper than comparing across different datasets. (Not perfectly controlled — they used Qwen3-4B, you're using Llama-3.2 models — but the data axis is clean.)

This makes GANIT access your single highest-priority Week 1 task. Email the authors early.

## Third: how the three LIMO/s1 criteria have to change for Bengali

Here's what the original recipes actually do, and where each one breaks:

**Quality.** s1 dropped items with API errors, broken formatting, ASCII art, references to missing images, and inconsistent numbering — going from 59K to about 51.5K before any difficulty filtering. For Bengali you need all of that *plus* checks the English papers never needed: is the problem actually in Bengali throughout (not half-English), are the numerals consistent (Bengali ০১২৩ versus Western 0123 — mixed numerals inside one problem are common in translated Bengali data and will confuse the model), and is the mathematical notation intact after translation. Machine translation is specifically known to mangle mathematical expressions, quantities, and logical dependencies, so this isn't optional cleanup.

**Difficulty — and this is where it gets genuinely tricky.** LIMO kept problems that a strong model solved in under 10% of attempts (excluding anything solved within four tries). s1 used two Qwen models and dropped anything either one got right, plus used reasoning-trace length as a second difficulty signal.

The trap: if you run that filter on Bengali problems, "hard" no longer means "mathematically hard" — it means "hard for this model, in Bengali." A trivial arithmetic problem the model fails only because it can't parse the Bengali sentence would be marked difficult and selected. You'd end up curating a set of *linguistically* confusing problems rather than mathematically deep ones, which is not what LIMO's hypothesis is about.

My recommendation: measure difficulty **two ways** and compare. Use GANIT's existing pass@k tags as your primary signal, and for the subset that has English parallels (SOMADHAN's items descend from GSM8K, so parallels exist), also compute difficulty on the English version. Then check how well the two rankings agree. If they diverge sharply, that disagreement is *itself* a reportable finding — it's a small, self-contained answer to the question you cut when you dropped LESS: do English-derived selection criteria actually identify valuable Bengali training examples? You'd get that contribution back almost for free.

Also note s1's trace-length signal doesn't transfer directly. Bengali is less token-efficient than English under most tokenizers, so a length threshold tuned on English traces will systematically mis-rank Bengali ones. Normalize by tokenizer, or use relative length within your own pool rather than an absolute cutoff.

**Diversity.** LIMO sampled across algebra, geometry, and proof-based problems from AIME, OlympiadBench, and Gaokao, deliberately keeping about 30% out-of-distribution. s1 used domain-stratified sampling. For you: stratify across the mathematical topics present in GANIT, and — since RQ2 is about transfer — deliberately keep the topic spread wide rather than letting it collapse onto arithmetic word problems. A set that's 90% grade-school arithmetic will almost certainly fail to transfer to B-REASO, and you won't be able to tell whether that's a real finding about SFT or just an artifact of narrow training data.

## Fourth: drop PatiGonit from the training set

I listed it as a source earlier; researching the criteria properly, it doesn't fit. PatiGonit is explicitly simple equation-based problems, many with a single operation. LIMO's whole difficulty filter exists to *remove* problems like that. Including them would work directly against the method.

Keep it, but repurpose it: use PatiGonit as an **easy-problem control set at evaluation time**. That gives you something valuable — Snell et al. found extra test-time compute helps mostly on easy questions rather than hard ones, and having an easy tier lets you check whether that pattern holds in Bengali. So it moves from training data to RQ3 evidence.

## The recipe, step by step

1. **Get GANIT access.** Highest priority. Everything downstream is easier if you have it.
2. **Pool candidates** from GANIT's CoT-SFT split, plus SOMADHAN's 4,000 human-annotated items *if* the contamination check clears.
3. **Cross-lingual decontamination first**, before any other filtering — trace every item to its English ancestor and drop anything descending from GSM8K test, MGSM's 250, or GSM-Plus's seeds. Then n-gram check as backup.
4. **Quality filter:** formatting, numeral consistency, language purity (fully Bengali), intact math notation. Manually inspect a random sample rather than trusting automated checks alone.
5. **Difficulty filter:** keep items with low pass@k. Compute difficulty both in Bengali and (where parallels exist) in English; record both, report the disagreement.
6. **Diversity sample:** stratify across topic and difficulty tier to hit your target count. Don't let one topic dominate.
7. **Verify the traces themselves** — read a sample by hand. Confirm the Bengali reasoning is actually coherent and actually leads to the stated answer. s1's own s1K traces were only about 53.6% correct because they optimized for reasoning length over accuracy; you don't want to inherit that problem silently.
8. **Freeze the set and publish the ID list**, so all three models provably get the identical data.

## One addition worth making: treat the size as a variable, not a constant

The "When Models Reason in Your Language" study post-trained on **100, 250, 500, and 817** instances per language and saw effects even at 100. Since your models are small and LoRA runs are fast, you could train at several sizes rather than just 1,000 — say 100 / 250 / 1000.

That turns "we picked 1,000 because LIMO did" into an actual data-efficiency curve for Bengali, which directly tests the less-is-more hypothesis instead of assuming it. It costs you more runs (3 models × 3 sizes = 9 instead of 3), but on 1B/3B LoRA that's very manageable, and it's the kind of result that makes a paper harder to dismiss. If time gets tight, drop it — but it's the cheapest strength you can add.

## One warning from the literature to design around

The multilingual distillation work found that SFT on translated traces **causes severe repetition problems in some languages**, and that translated traces can mismatch the model's own natural reasoning style. Your manual trace audit in Week 8 is where you'd catch this — but plan for the possibility that a model comes out fluent-looking and stuck in loops. Prefer GANIT's natively-Bengali CoT over machine-translated traces wherever you have the choice, precisely because of this.

# Ganit Dataset Overview

## Creator and Purpose
The Ganit dataset was created by Shubhashis Roy Dipta and colleagues as "a rigorously-processed, difficulty-aware Bengali mathematical reasoning dataset designed for training and evaluating LLMs on Bengali math problems." It represents the first Bengali mathematics dataset incorporating difficulty stratification.

## Content and Structure
Ganit contains Bengali mathematics problems with solutions in both Bengali and English numerals. The dataset encompasses approximately 19,127 total examples across three splits:

- **GanitSFT**: 11,023 examples for supervised fine-tuning
- **GanitRLVR**: 7,328 examples for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards
- **GanitDEV**: 776 examples for evaluation

## Language and Reasoning
All problems are presented in Bengali with "chain-of-thought reasoning" included. The dataset requires "Bengali CoT" for supervised fine-tuning and enables "reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards."

## Difficulty Classification
Problems are stratified into four tiers—easy, medium, hard, and olympiad—based on pass@32 scores from language model evaluations. The development set maintains balanced representation: "Easy: 28.7%, Medium: 26.0%, Hard: 24.3%, Olympiad: 21.3%."

## Sources and Processing
Ganit aggregates data from five sources including NuminaMath-CoT-bn, SOMADHAN, and mCoT-MATH-bn. The creation process involved "quality screening," deduplication, decontamination against benchmarks, and difficulty tagging through model generation.

## Licensing and Citation
Released under the Apache 2.0 License, the dataset is associated with the paper "GanitLLM: Difficulty-Aware Bengali Mathematical Reasoning through Curriculum-GRPO" (arXiv:2601.06767), accepted at ACL 2026 Findings.

"""
Curate a LIMO-style minimal training set from the Ganit Bengali math dataset.

Pipeline: explore -> decontaminate -> difficulty filter -> dedup -> stratified
sample -> freeze.

Every stage is parameterised so the whole thing can be re-run at different
difficulty windows and set sizes for the ablations, and `--seed` keeps the
selection reproducible.

Usage:
    # 1. Look at the pool before deciding anything
    python ganit_curate.py --explore-only

    # 2. LIMO's own threshold (<10% solve rate == 1-3 correct out of 32)
    python ganit_curate.py --min-correct 1 --max-correct 3 --n 1000

    # 3. Wider Hard+Olympiad window, likelier to suit 1B/3B models
    python ganit_curate.py --min-correct 1 --max-correct 16 --n 1000

    # 4. Size ablation
    python ganit_curate.py --min-correct 1 --max-correct 16 --n 100
    python ganit_curate.py --min-correct 1 --max-correct 16 --n 250

Decontamination against the eval benchmarks needs their problem text as a
newline-delimited .txt or a .jsonl with a "problem"/"question" field:

    python ganit_curate.py --n 1000 \
        --contaminants bn_mgsm.jsonl gsm_plus_bn.jsonl bennumeval.jsonl
"""

import argparse
import hashlib
import json
import random
import re
import sys
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
from pathlib import Path

try:
    from datasets import load_dataset
except ImportError:
    sys.exit("Missing dependency. Run:  pip install datasets")


DATASET_ID = "dipta007/Ganit"
SFT_SPLIT = "GanitSFT"
TOTAL_SAMPLES = 32  # Ganit scored every problem with 32 generations from Qwen3-32B

# Bengali digits U+09E6..U+09EF map onto 0-9. Ganit carries solutions in both
# Bengali and Western numerals, and translated sources mix them inside a single
# problem, so everything is normalised to Western before any matching.
BN_DIGITS = str.maketrans("০১২৩৪৫৬৭৮৯", "0123456789")

NUMBER_RE = re.compile(r"\d+(?:\.\d+)?")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# normalisation and fingerprinting
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def normalise(text):
    """Lowercase, convert Bengali digits, collapse whitespace and punctuation."""
    if not text:
        return ""
    text = text.translate(BN_DIGITS).lower()
    text = re.sub(r"[^\w\s.]", " ", text)
    return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text).strip()


def numeric_fingerprint(text):
    """
    Sorted multiset of the numbers in a problem, as a hash.

    This is the part that matters for cross-lingual decontamination. Ganit was
    decontaminated with MinHash over Bengali surface text, which cannot catch a
    problem that reaches two benchmarks through two independent translations --
    different words, same problem. The numbers survive translation, so for math
    word problems they fingerprint the underlying item far better than n-grams.

    Deliberately loose: it over-flags rather than under-flags, and anything it
    catches is meant to be eyeballed before removal (see --review-flagged).
    """
    nums = NUMBER_RE.findall(normalise(text))
    if not nums:
        return None
    # Trailing .0 normalised away so "5" and "5.0" fingerprint alike.
    canon = sorted(str(float(n)).rstrip("0").rstrip(".") for n in nums)
    return hashlib.md5("|".join(canon).encode()).hexdigest()


def token_set(text):
    return set(normalise(text).split())


def jaccard(a, b):
    if not a or not b:
        return 0.0
    return len(a & b) / len(a | b)


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# stages
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def explore(rows):
    """Print the distributions that decide every threshold downstream."""
    print(f"\nPool: {len(rows)} rows from {DATASET_ID} [{SFT_SPLIT}]\n")

    print("By difficulty tier")
    for tier, n in Counter(r["difficulty"] for r in rows).most_common():
        print(f"  {str(tier):<12} {n:>6}  ({n / len(rows):5.1%})")

    print("\nBy source")
    for src, n in Counter(r["source_name"] for r in rows).most_common():
        print(f"  {str(src):<24} {n:>6}  ({n / len(rows):5.1%})")

    print(f"\nBy correct_counts (out of {TOTAL_SAMPLES})")
    counts = Counter(r["correct_counts"] for r in rows)
    cumulative = 0
    for c in sorted(counts):
        cumulative += counts[c]
        marker = "  <- LIMO window (<10% solve rate)" if c <= 3 else ""
        print(f"  {c:>3}/{TOTAL_SAMPLES}  {counts[c]:>5}   cum {cumulative:>6}{marker}")

    limo_pool = sum(n for c, n in counts.items() if 1 <= c <= 3)
    print(f"\nItems in LIMO's strict window (1-3 correct): {limo_pool}")
    if limo_pool < 1000:
        print("  NOTE: fewer than 1000 available at LIMO's threshold. Either widen")
        print("  the window (--max-correct) or accept a smaller set. Widening is")
        print("  likely the better call anyway -- difficulty here was scored by")
        print("  Qwen3-32B, which is 10-30x larger than the models being trained.")


def load_contaminants(paths):
    """Read benchmark problem text from .txt (one per line) or .jsonl."""
    items = []
    for path in paths:
        p = Path(path)
        if not p.exists():
            print(f"  WARNING: {path} not found, skipping")
            continue
        if p.suffix == ".jsonl":
            for line in p.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines():
                if not line.strip():
                    continue
                obj = json.loads(line)
                text = obj.get("problem") or obj.get("question") or obj.get("text")
                if text:
                    items.append((p.name, text))
        else:
            items.extend(
                (p.name, ln) for ln in p.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines() if ln.strip()
            )
        print(f"  loaded {path}")
    return items


def decontaminate(rows, contaminants, jaccard_threshold=0.7):
    """
    Drop pool items that collide with any eval benchmark.

    Two independent signals:
      1. numeric fingerprint  -- translation-invariant, catches re-translations
      2. token Jaccard        -- catches near-copies sharing wording

    Fingerprint hits are reported separately because they are the interesting
    ones: those are exactly the items Ganit's MinHash pass would have missed.
    """
    if not contaminants:
        print("\nNo contaminant files given -- SKIPPING decontamination.")
        print("Do not report final numbers from a run without this step.")
        print("Ganit was only decontaminated against Bn-MGSM and Bn-MSVAMP, so")
        print("GSM-Plus-BN, BenNumEval and B-REASO are unchecked.")
        return rows, []

    bench_fp = defaultdict(list)
    bench_tokens = []
    for name, text in contaminants:
        fp = numeric_fingerprint(text)
        if fp:
            bench_fp[fp].append((name, text))
        bench_tokens.append((name, text, token_set(text)))

    kept, flagged = [], []
    for row in rows:
        problem = row["problem"]
        hit = None

        fp = numeric_fingerprint(problem)
        if fp and fp in bench_fp:
            src_name, src_text = bench_fp[fp][0]
            hit = ("numeric_fingerprint", src_name, src_text, 1.0)

        if hit is None:
            tokens = token_set(problem)
            for src_name, src_text, src_tokens in bench_tokens:
                sim = jaccard(tokens, src_tokens)
                if sim >= jaccard_threshold:
                    hit = ("token_jaccard", src_name, src_text, sim)
                    break

        if hit:
            flagged.append({
                "idx": row["_idx"],
                "problem": problem,
                "method": hit[0],
                "benchmark": hit[1],
                "matched_text": hit[2],
                "similarity": hit[3],
            })
        else:
            kept.append(row)

    by_method = Counter(f["method"] for f in flagged)
    print(f"\nDecontamination: removed {len(flagged)}, kept {len(kept)}")
    for method, n in by_method.most_common():
        print(f"  {method:<22} {n}")
    if by_method.get("numeric_fingerprint"):
        print("  ^ these are the cross-lingual duplicates MinHash misses -- worth")
        print("    a line in the paper.")
    return kept, flagged


def difficulty_filter(rows, min_correct, max_correct):
    kept = [r for r in rows if min_correct <= r["correct_counts"] <= max_correct]
    pct_lo = 100 * min_correct / TOTAL_SAMPLES
    pct_hi = 100 * max_correct / TOTAL_SAMPLES
    print(f"\nDifficulty window {min_correct}-{max_correct}/{TOTAL_SAMPLES} "
          f"({pct_lo:.0f}%-{pct_hi:.0f}% solve rate): {len(kept)} items")
    return kept


def dedup(rows, jaccard_threshold=0.8):
    """
    Drop near-duplicates inside the pool.

    Diversity control, LIMO-style. Ganit has no topic field, so topic-stratified
    sampling is not possible; removing near-identical problems is the practical
    stand-in and stops the set filling with variants of one template.
    """
    seen_fp = {}
    kept, dropped = [], 0
    for row in rows:
        fp = numeric_fingerprint(row["problem"])
        tokens = token_set(row["problem"])
        is_dup = False

        if fp and fp in seen_fp:
            for other in seen_fp[fp]:
                if jaccard(tokens, other) >= jaccard_threshold:
                    is_dup = True
                    break

        if is_dup:
            dropped += 1
        else:
            kept.append(row)
            if fp:
                seen_fp.setdefault(fp, []).append(tokens)

    print(f"Near-duplicate removal: dropped {dropped}, kept {len(kept)}")
    return kept


def stratified_sample(rows, n, seed, somadhan_floor=0.0):
    """
    Sample n items keeping the source mix roughly proportional.

    `somadhan_floor` optionally guarantees a minimum share of human-translated
    SOMADHAN items. GanitSFT is ~71% machine-translated NuminaMath-CoT-bn, and
    SFT on translated traces is a documented cause of repetition loops and
    code-switching -- both of which are dependent variables here, so the mix
    should be a controlled choice rather than an accident.
    """
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    if n >= len(rows):
        print(f"\nRequested {n} but only {len(rows)} available -- taking all.")
        return list(rows)

    by_source = defaultdict(list)
    for row in rows:
        by_source[row["source_name"]].append(row)
    for bucket in by_source.values():
        rng.shuffle(bucket)

    selected = []

    if somadhan_floor > 0:
        key = next((s for s in by_source if "somadhan" in str(s).lower()), None)
        if key:
            want = min(int(n * somadhan_floor), len(by_source[key]))
            selected.extend(by_source[key][:want])
            by_source[key] = by_source[key][want:]
            print(f"\nSOMADHAN floor: {want} items ({want / n:.0%} of target)")
        else:
            print("\nWARNING: --somadhan-floor set but no SOMADHAN source found.")

    remaining = n - len(selected)
    pool_left = sum(len(v) for v in by_source.values())
    if pool_left:
        for src, bucket in by_source.items():
            take = min(round(remaining * len(bucket) / pool_left), len(bucket))
            selected.extend(bucket[:take])

    # Proportional rounding can land a few over or under.
    if len(selected) > n:
        rng.shuffle(selected)
        selected = selected[:n]
    elif len(selected) < n:
        chosen = {r["_idx"] for r in selected}
        spare = [r for r in rows if r["_idx"] not in chosen]
        rng.shuffle(spare)
        selected.extend(spare[: n - len(selected)])

    rng.shuffle(selected)
    return selected


def report(selected):
    print(f"\n--- Selected {len(selected)} ---")
    print("By source")
    for src, n in Counter(r["source_name"] for r in selected).most_common():
        print(f"  {str(src):<24} {n:>5}  ({n / len(selected):5.1%})")
    print("By difficulty tier")
    for tier, n in Counter(r["difficulty"] for r in selected).most_common():
        print(f"  {str(tier):<12} {n:>5}  ({n / len(selected):5.1%})")
    cc = [r["correct_counts"] for r in selected]
    print(f"correct_counts: min {min(cc)}, max {max(cc)}, mean {sum(cc) / len(cc):.1f}")


def freeze(selected, flagged, args, out_dir):
    """
    Write the frozen selection.

    The ID list is the artefact that matters: it is what makes "all three models
    saw identical data" checkable by a reviewer, and what gets released with the
    paper.
    """
    out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    tag = f"n{args.n}_c{args.min_correct}-{args.max_correct}_seed{args.seed}"

    ids_path = out_dir / f"ganit_limo_{tag}.ids.json"
    ids_path.write_text(json.dumps({
        "dataset": DATASET_ID,
        "split": SFT_SPLIT,
        "n": len(selected),
        "params": vars(args),
        "row_indices": sorted(r["_idx"] for r in selected),
    }, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")

    data_path = out_dir / f"ganit_limo_{tag}.jsonl"
    with data_path.open("w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        for row in selected:
            fh.write(json.dumps({
                "idx": row["_idx"],
                "problem": row["problem"],
                "bengali_solution": row["bengali_solution"],
                "messages": row["messages"],
                "difficulty": row["difficulty"],
                "correct_counts": row["correct_counts"],
                "source_name": row["source_name"],
            }, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")

    print(f"\nWrote {ids_path}")
    print(f"Wrote {data_path}")

    if flagged:
        flag_path = out_dir / f"decontamination_flagged_{tag}.jsonl"
        with flag_path.open("w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
            for item in flagged:
                fh.write(json.dumps(item, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")
        print(f"Wrote {flag_path}  <- read these before trusting the removals")

    audit_path = out_dir / f"audit_sample_{tag}.jsonl"
    rng = random.Random(args.seed)
    with audit_path.open("w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        for row in rng.sample(selected, min(30, len(selected))):
            fh.write(json.dumps({
                "idx": row["_idx"],
                "problem": row["problem"],
                "bengali_solution": row["bengali_solution"],
                "source_name": row["source_name"],
                "correct_counts": row["correct_counts"],
                "_check_reasoning_is_coherent": None,
                "_check_stays_in_bengali": None,
                "_check_reaches_stated_answer": None,
            }, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")
    print(f"Wrote {audit_path}  <- 30 traces to read by hand, fill the _check_ fields")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__,
                                 formatter_class=argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter)
    ap.add_argument("--explore-only", action="store_true",
                    help="print pool distributions and exit")
    ap.add_argument("--n", type=int, default=1000, help="target set size")
    ap.add_argument("--min-correct", type=int, default=1,
                    help="min correct_counts out of 32 (0 excludes unsolvable)")
    ap.add_argument("--max-correct", type=int, default=16,
                    help="max correct_counts; 3 = LIMO's strict <10%% window")
    ap.add_argument("--somadhan-floor", type=float, default=0.0,
                    help="min share of human-translated SOMADHAN, e.g. 0.4")
    ap.add_argument("--contaminants", nargs="*", default=[],
                    help="benchmark files (.jsonl or .txt) to decontaminate against")
    ap.add_argument("--no-dedup", action="store_true")
    ap.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=42)
    ap.add_argument("--out", default="curated")
    args = ap.parse_args()

    print(f"Loading {DATASET_ID} [{SFT_SPLIT}] ...")
    ds = load_dataset(DATASET_ID, split=SFT_SPLIT)
    rows = [{**row, "_idx": i} for i, row in enumerate(ds)]

    explore(rows)
    if args.explore_only:
        print("\nExplore only. Pick --min-correct/--max-correct from the table above.")
        return

    contaminants = load_contaminants(args.contaminants) if args.contaminants else []
    rows, flagged = decontaminate(rows, contaminants)

    rows = difficulty_filter(rows, args.min_correct, args.max_correct)
    if not rows:
        sys.exit("Nothing left after difficulty filtering -- widen the window.")

    if not args.no_dedup:
        rows = dedup(rows)

    selected = stratified_sample(rows, args.n, args.seed, args.somadhan_floor)
    report(selected)
    freeze(selected, flagged, args, Path(args.out))

    print("\nNext: read the audit sample before training on any of this.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

    different words, same problem. The numbers survive translation, so for math
    word problems they fingerprint the underlying item far better than n-grams.

    Deliberately loose: it over-flags rather than under-flags, and anything it
    catches is meant to be eyeballed before removal (see --review-flagged).
    """
    nums = NUMBER_RE.findall(normalise(text))
    if not nums:
        return None
    # Trailing .0 normalised away so "5" and "5.0" fingerprint alike.
    canon = sorted(str(float(n)).rstrip("0").rstrip(".") for n in nums)
    return hashlib.md5("|".join(canon).encode()).hexdigest()


def token_set(text):
    return set(normalise(text).split())


def jaccard(a, b):
    if not a or not b:
        return 0.0
    return len(a & b) / len(a | b)


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# stages
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def explore(rows):
    """Print the distributions that decide every threshold downstream."""
    print(f"\nPool: {len(rows)} rows from {DATASET_ID} [{SFT_SPLIT}]\n")

    print("By difficulty tier")
    for tier, n in Counter(r["difficulty"] for r in rows).most_common():
        print(f"  {str(tier):<12} {n:>6}  ({n / len(rows):5.1%})")

    print("\nBy source")
    for src, n in Counter(r["source_name"] for r in rows).most_common():
        print(f"  {str(src):<24} {n:>6}  ({n / len(rows):5.1%})")

    print(f"\nBy correct_counts (out of {TOTAL_SAMPLES})")
    counts = Counter(r["correct_counts"] for r in rows)
    cumulative = 0
    for c in sorted(counts):
        cumulative += counts[c]
        marker = "  <- LIMO window (<10% solve rate)" if c <= 3 else ""
        print(f"  {c:>3}/{TOTAL_SAMPLES}  {counts[c]:>5}   cum {cumulative:>6}{marker}")

    limo_pool = sum(n for c, n in counts.items() if 1 <= c <= 3)
    print(f"\nItems in LIMO's strict window (1-3 correct): {limo_pool}")
    if limo_pool < 1000:
        print("  NOTE: fewer than 1000 available at LIMO's threshold. Either widen")
        print("  the window (--max-correct) or accept a smaller set. Widening is")
        print("  likely the better call anyway -- difficulty here was scored by")
        print("  Qwen3-32B, which is 10-30x larger than the models being trained.")


def load_contaminants(paths):
    """Read benchmark problem text from .txt (one per line) or .jsonl."""
    items = []
    for path in paths:
        p = Path(path)
        if not p.exists():
            print(f"  WARNING: {path} not found, skipping")
            continue
        if p.suffix == ".jsonl":
            for line in p.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines():
                if not line.strip():
                    continue
                obj = json.loads(line)
                text = obj.get("problem") or obj.get("question") or obj.get("text")
                if text:
                    items.append((p.name, text))
        else:
            items.extend(
                (p.name, ln) for ln in p.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines() if ln.strip()
            )
        print(f"  loaded {path}")
    return items


def decontaminate(rows, contaminants, jaccard_threshold=0.7):
    """
    Drop pool items that collide with any eval benchmark.

    Two independent signals:
      1. numeric fingerprint  -- translation-invariant, catches re-translations
      2. token Jaccard        -- catches near-copies sharing wording

    Fingerprint hits are reported separately because they are the interesting
    ones: those are exactly the items Ganit's MinHash pass would have missed.
    """
    if not contaminants:
        print("\nNo contaminant files given -- SKIPPING decontamination.")
        print("Do not report final numbers from a run without this step.")
        print("Ganit was only decontaminated against Bn-MGSM and Bn-MSVAMP, so")
        print("GSM-Plus-BN, BenNumEval and B-REASO are unchecked.")
        return rows, []

    bench_fp = defaultdict(list)
    bench_tokens = []
    for name, text in contaminants:
        fp = numeric_fingerprint(text)
        if fp:
            bench_fp[fp].append((name, text))
        bench_tokens.append((name, text, token_set(text)))

    kept, flagged = [], []
    for row in rows:
        problem = row["problem"]
        hit = None

        fp = numeric_fingerprint(problem)
        if fp and fp in bench_fp:
            src_name, src_text = bench_fp[fp][0]
            hit = ("numeric_fingerprint", src_name, src_text, 1.0)

        if hit is None:
            tokens = token_set(problem)
            for src_name, src_text, src_tokens in bench_tokens:
                sim = jaccard(tokens, src_tokens)
                if sim >= jaccard_threshold:
                    hit = ("token_jaccard", src_name, src_text, sim)
                    break

        if hit:
            flagged.append({
                "idx": row["_idx"],
                "problem": problem,
                "method": hit[0],
                "benchmark": hit[1],
                "matched_text": hit[2],
                "similarity": hit[3],
            })
        else:
            kept.append(row)

    by_method = Counter(f["method"] for f in flagged)
    print(f"\nDecontamination: removed {len(flagged)}, kept {len(kept)}")
    for method, n in by_method.most_common():
        print(f"  {method:<22} {n}")
    if by_method.get("numeric_fingerprint"):
        print("  ^ these are the cross-lingual duplicates MinHash misses -- worth")
        print("    a line in the paper.")
    return kept, flagged


def difficulty_filter(rows, min_correct, max_correct):
    kept = [r for r in rows if min_correct <= r["correct_counts"] <= max_correct]
    pct_lo = 100 * min_correct / TOTAL_SAMPLES
    pct_hi = 100 * max_correct / TOTAL_SAMPLES
    print(f"\nDifficulty window {min_correct}-{max_correct}/{TOTAL_SAMPLES} "
          f"({pct_lo:.0f}%-{pct_hi:.0f}% solve rate): {len(kept)} items")
    return kept


def dedup(rows, jaccard_threshold=0.8):
    """
    Drop near-duplicates inside the pool.

    Diversity control, LIMO-style. Ganit has no topic field, so topic-stratified
    sampling is not possible; removing near-identical problems is the practical
    stand-in and stops the set filling with variants of one template.
    """
    seen_fp = {}
    kept, dropped = [], 0
    for row in rows:
        fp = numeric_fingerprint(row["problem"])
        tokens = token_set(row["problem"])
        is_dup = False

        if fp and fp in seen_fp:
            for other in seen_fp[fp]:
                if jaccard(tokens, other) >= jaccard_threshold:
                    is_dup = True
                    break

        if is_dup:
            dropped += 1
        else:
            kept.append(row)
            if fp:
                seen_fp.setdefault(fp, []).append(tokens)

    print(f"Near-duplicate removal: dropped {dropped}, kept {len(kept)}")
    return kept


def stratified_sample(rows, n, seed, somadhan_floor=0.0):
    """
    Sample n items keeping the source mix roughly proportional.

    `somadhan_floor` optionally guarantees a minimum share of human-translated
    SOMADHAN items. GanitSFT is ~71% machine-translated NuminaMath-CoT-bn, and
    SFT on translated traces is a documented cause of repetition loops and
    code-switching -- both of which are dependent variables here, so the mix
    should be a controlled choice rather than an accident.
    """
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    if n >= len(rows):
        print(f"\nRequested {n} but only {len(rows)} available -- taking all.")
        return list(rows)

    by_source = defaultdict(list)
    for row in rows:
        by_source[row["source_name"]].append(row)
    for bucket in by_source.values():
        rng.shuffle(bucket)

    selected = []

    if somadhan_floor > 0:
        key = next((s for s in by_source if "somadhan" in str(s).lower()), None)
        if key:
            want = min(int(n * somadhan_floor), len(by_source[key]))
            selected.extend(by_source[key][:want])
            by_source[key] = by_source[key][want:]
            print(f"\nSOMADHAN floor: {want} items ({want / n:.0%} of target)")
        else:
            print("\nWARNING: --somadhan-floor set but no SOMADHAN source found.")

    remaining = n - len(selected)
    pool_left = sum(len(v) for v in by_source.values())
    if pool_left:
        for src, bucket in by_source.items():
            take = min(round(remaining * len(bucket) / pool_left), len(bucket))
            selected.extend(bucket[:take])

    # Proportional rounding can land a few over or under.
    if len(selected) > n:
        rng.shuffle(selected)
        selected = selected[:n]
    elif len(selected) < n:
        chosen = {r["_idx"] for r in selected}
        spare = [r for r in rows if r["_idx"] not in chosen]
        rng.shuffle(spare)
        selected.extend(spare[: n - len(selected)])

    rng.shuffle(selected)
    return selected


def report(selected):
    print(f"\n--- Selected {len(selected)} ---")
    print("By source")
    for src, n in Counter(r["source_name"] for r in selected).most_common():
        print(f"  {str(src):<24} {n:>5}  ({n / len(selected):5.1%})")
    print("By difficulty tier")
    for tier, n in Counter(r["difficulty"] for r in selected).most_common():
        print(f"  {str(tier):<12} {n:>5}  ({n / len(selected):5.1%})")
    cc = [r["correct_counts"] for r in selected]
    print(f"correct_counts: min {min(cc)}, max {max(cc)}, mean {sum(cc) / len(cc):.1f}")


def freeze(selected, flagged, args, out_dir):
    """
    Write the frozen selection.

    The ID list is the artefact that matters: it is what makes "all three models
    saw identical data" checkable by a reviewer, and what gets released with the
    paper.
    """
    out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    tag = f"n{args.n}_c{args.min_correct}-{args.max_correct}_seed{args.seed}"

    ids_path = out_dir / f"ganit_limo_{tag}.ids.json"
    ids_path.write_text(json.dumps({
        "dataset": DATASET_ID,
        "split": SFT_SPLIT,
        "n": len(selected),
        "params": vars(args),
        "row_indices": sorted(r["_idx"] for r in selected),
    }, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")

    data_path = out_dir / f"ganit_limo_{tag}.jsonl"
    with data_path.open("w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        for row in selected:
            fh.write(json.dumps({
                "idx": row["_idx"],
                "problem": row["problem"],
                "bengali_solution": row["bengali_solution"],
                "messages": row["messages"],
                "difficulty": row["difficulty"],
                "correct_counts": row["correct_counts"],
                "source_name": row["source_name"],
            }, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")

    print(f"\nWrote {ids_path}")
    print(f"Wrote {data_path}")

    if flagged:
        flag_path = out_dir / f"decontamination_flagged_{tag}.jsonl"
        with flag_path.open("w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
            for item in flagged:
                fh.write(json.dumps(item, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")
        print(f"Wrote {flag_path}  <- read these before trusting the removals")

    audit_path = out_dir / f"audit_sample_{tag}.jsonl"
    rng = random.Random(args.seed)
    with audit_path.open("w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        for row in rng.sample(selected, min(30, len(selected))):
            fh.write(json.dumps({
                "idx": row["_idx"],
                "problem": row["problem"],
                "bengali_solution": row["bengali_solution"],
                "source_name": row["source_name"],
                "correct_counts": row["correct_counts"],
                "_check_reasoning_is_coherent": None,
                "_check_stays_in_bengali": None,
                "_check_reaches_stated_answer": None,
            }, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")
    print(f"Wrote {audit_path}  <- 30 traces to read by hand, fill the _check_ fields")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__,
                                 formatter_class=argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter)
    ap.add_argument("--explore-only", action="store_true",
                    help="print pool distributions and exit")
    ap.add_argument("--n", type=int, default=1000, help="target set size")
    ap.add_argument("--min-correct", type=int, default=1,
                    help="min correct_counts out of 32 (0 excludes unsolvable)")
    ap.add_argument("--max-correct", type=int, default=16,
                    help="max correct_counts; 3 = LIMO's strict <10%% window")
    ap.add_argument("--somadhan-floor", type=float, default=0.0,
                    help="min share of human-translated SOMADHAN, e.g. 0.4")
    ap.add_argument("--contaminants", nargs="*", default=[],
                    help="benchmark files (.jsonl or .txt) to decontaminate against")
    ap.add_argument("--no-dedup", action="store_true")
    ap.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=42)
    ap.add_argument("--out", default="curated")
    args = ap.parse_args()

    print(f"Loading {DATASET_ID} [{SFT_SPLIT}] ...")
    ds = load_dataset(DATASET_ID, split=SFT_SPLIT)
    rows = [{**row, "_idx": i} for i, row in enumerate(ds)]

    explore(rows)
    if args.explore_only:
        print("\nExplore only. Pick --min-correct/--max-correct from the table above.")
        return

    contaminants = load_contaminants(args.contaminants) if args.contaminants else []
    rows, flagged = decontaminate(rows, contaminants)

    rows = difficulty_filter(rows, args.min_correct, args.max_correct)
    if not rows:
        sys.exit("Nothing left after difficulty filtering -- widen the window.")

    if not args.no_dedup:
        rows = dedup(rows)

    selected = stratified_sample(rows, args.n, args.seed, args.somadhan_floor)
    report(selected)
    freeze(selected, flagged, args, Path(args.out))

    print("\nNext: read the audit sample before training on any of this.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

1	"""
2	Curate a LIMO-style minimal training set from the Ganit Bengali math dataset.
3	
4	Pipeline: explore -> decontaminate -> difficulty filter -> dedup -> stratified
5	sample -> freeze.
6	
7	Every stage is parameterised so the whole thing can be re-run at different
8	difficulty windows and set sizes for the ablations, and `--seed` keeps the
9	selection reproducible.
10	
11	Usage:
12	    # 1. Look at the pool before deciding anything
13	    python ganit_curate.py --explore-only
14	
15	    # 2. LIMO's own threshold (<10% solve rate == 1-3 correct out of 32)
16	    python ganit_curate.py --min-correct 1 --max-correct 3 --n 1000
17	
18	    # 3. Wider Hard+Olympiad window, likelier to suit 1B/3B models
19	    python ganit_curate.py --min-correct 1 --max-correct 16 --n 1000
20	
21	    # 4. Size ablation
22	    python ganit_curate.py --min-correct 1 --max-correct 16 --n 100
23	    python ganit_curate.py --min-correct 1 --max-correct 16 --n 250
24	
25	Decontamination against the eval benchmarks needs their problem text as a
26	newline-delimited .txt or a .jsonl with a "problem"/"question" field:
27	
28	    python ganit_curate.py --n 1000 \
29	        --contaminants bn_mgsm.jsonl gsm_plus_bn.jsonl bennumeval.jsonl
30	"""
31	
32	import argparse

content.text:
Script works end to end. Files are in `D:\791\curated\`. But running it against the real data overturned several things I told you from the dataset card — the card is out of date.

## What's actually in there (card vs. reality)

| | Card said | Actually |
|---|---|---|
| SFT pool | 11,023 | **16,868** |
| numina-math-cot-bn | 7,827 (71%) | **13,160 (78%)** |
| SOMADHAN | 3,039 | **3,487 (20.7%)** |
| s1k-32-Bangla | "not in SFT" | **28 items, and they are in SFT** |

Also, the field I told you to train on was wrong. **`bengali_solution` is just the final answer** (median 2 characters — e.g. `'৬৭৩০.২'`). The actual reasoning traces live in **`messages`**, as a user/assistant pair, median ~1,148 characters. The script now trains on `messages` and keeps `bengali_solution` only for answer-checking. It also freezes on the dataset's own `id` field rather than row index, which is stable across reloads.

## Three findings that change your design

**1. The difficulty distribution is barely usable for curation.** It's extremely bimodal — 5,645 items at 0/32 (33.5%) and 8,562 at 32/32 (50.8%). Over 84% of the dataset is "the model always got it right" or "always got it wrong." The middle, where difficulty-based selection actually has signal, is nearly empty: the entire 1–16 band is only 1,025 items.

That means **LIMO's strict window (1–3 correct) yields just 681 items — you cannot reach 1,000.** And at the widened 1–16 window, taking 1,000 uses 97.6% of everything eligible. That isn't curation, it's taking almost the whole pool.

**2. The 0/32 band is contaminated with broken data, not just hard data.** 404 of those items come from SOMADHAN — which is translated GSM8K, i.e. grade-school word problems. A 32B model failing grade-school arithmetic 32 times out of 32 doesn't mean the problem is hard; it means the gold answer or the translation is broken. numina-math-cot-bn is also over-represented there (91.7% of the 0/32 band versus 78% of the pool). Keep `--min-correct 1` — excluding 0/32 is essential, not optional.

(Separately: all 28 s1k-32-Bangla items sit at 0/32, which makes sense — s1K is deliberately brutal competition problems. Too few to use, but it confirms the band does contain genuinely hard items mixed in with the broken ones.)

**3. You cannot have "hard" and "human-translated" at the same time.** I set a 40% SOMADHAN floor and it could only deliver 13.6% — because SOMADHAN is GSM8K-derived and therefore mostly easy, so almost none of it survives a difficulty filter. Your hard subset is unavoidably ~85% machine-translated NuminaMath.

That's a real tension, and it's worth reporting rather than hiding: in this dataset, difficulty and translation quality pull in opposite directions. Since Bengali language adherence is one of your dependent variables, and translated traces are the documented cause of repetition loops and code-switching, you should state plainly that your training set is predominantly machine-translated by necessity.

## What I'd do about the set size

Given only 1,025 eligible items, the n=1,000 target no longer makes much sense. Better options:

- **n = 681** at LIMO's exact threshold. This is close to LIMO's own 817, uses the strict criterion honestly, and lets you say you replicated their filter rather than approximating it. I'd lean here.
- **n = 250–500** at the wider window, which restores actual selectivity — you'd be choosing from 1,025, not taking all of it.
- Run **both plus n=100** as the size ablation. On 1B/3B LoRA this is cheap, and it converts a forced compromise into a data-efficiency curve, which is a better story than "we wanted 1,000 and got 1,025."
